correct_and_secure.verdict: Partly — no confirmed exploitable security hole, but one mechanism as specified cannot be built on the stack the doc mandates.
correct_and_secure.most_serious_defect: The per-entry leader signature (lines 301-305, 331-344): the leader must assign and sign (term, log_index, previous_entry_hash) BEFORE proposing to Raft, which no mainstream embedded Raft library permits — hashicorp/raft's Apply/ApplyLog and etcd/raft's Propose both seal the payload and assign term/index internally, with no index-reservation API. The only workaround is serializing every proposal against LastIndex()+1, which races leader no-op and configuration entries and forecloses the pipelining the line 889 benchmarks assume. Compounding it, the hash chain's domain is self-contradictory: previous_entry_hash sits in the leader-signed block (336) while line 367 says rejected commands and Raft config entries consume indices so accepted-event indices have gaps — if the chain covers all Raft entries a nonvoter receiving only accepted events (371) can never recompute it; if it covers accepted events only the leader provably cannot compute it at propose time, because acceptance is decided at apply (358-362). Safety is not broken (lines 88 and 303-305 make quorum commitment plus deterministic apply authoritative, so a signed-but-uncommitted entry never becomes history), so this is a feasibility and integrity-definition defect, not a vulnerability. The security layer as a whole is under-specified rather than wrong: no signature suite, hash, canonical encoding, or per-context domain separation is named anywhere (the only algorithm in the file is SHA-256 at line 572, for Git bundles), which blocks the golden-fixture merge gate at 815-819 but is legitimately queued as ADR-003.

done_well: The 2.4 invariant table is written as negative safety properties with a named enforcement mechanism per row ("No DB diffs on wire | Typed events/snapshots only; received SQL is inert data"). Most designs list positive aspirations; stating what MUST NOT happen and where it is prevented is what makes sections 5, 8, and 12 auditable against it.

The Syncthing containment design (533-544) is genuinely careful engineering, not boilerplate: per-authorized-pair local connector, mTLS CONNECT tunnel that can only forward to the receiver's own session-bound loopback sidecar, "No caller chooses a destination", Syncthing's own TLS retained inside the tunnel, and an explicit list of Syncthing features to disable (global discovery, relays, NAT mapping, introducers, auto-accept, self-update, peer-controlled config). The threat of "managed sidecar becomes an open proxy" was clearly reasoned about and closed.

The commit pipeline (352-369) gets the details that usually go wrong: event, rejection, idempotency result, projection, and applied index commit in ONE SQLite transaction; an invalid command stores the same structured rejection on every replica rather than diverging; index gaps from rejected and config entries are stated explicitly; and leader prevalidation is explicitly declared non-authoritative (369). Line 305 correctly puts both signatures on long-lived identity keys rather than rotating transport keys so history stays verifiable.

The refusal to synchronize .git/, SQLite pages/WAL, or Session Extension changesets (377-381) comes with the actual reasoning — leaks unrelated and deleted data, bypasses domain authorization, couples peers to page/schema/migration history. That is the correct call and the correct justification, and it is repeated as an ADR (ADR-018) rather than left implicit.

Section 12 is unusually strong for a design doc: "Do not mock SQLite or Raft when testing their behavior" (814), real three-voter Raft and real pinned Syncthing in the harness, the harness itself as a V1 deliverable (824), faults injected specifically at the Raft/SQLite boundaries (829-832), cross-replica projection-digest equality after quiescence (834), immutable golden fixtures with historical migration replay (817-819), and leaking test artifacts as a release blocker (908-909).

The doc is repeatedly honest about the limits of its own mechanisms rather than overselling them: leases "cannot stop a same-user process from editing a path" (442), "Signatures prove provenance, not content safety" (715), "MCP cannot observe every native action" (522), "CodeComm never claims arbitrary offline writes are mergeable" (451), and the three-voter requirement stated at 32, 61, 136, and 139-140. Risk 1 concedes that provenance and control paths cannot replace sandboxing.

Density. Roughly 1,000 lines carry a decided position on platforms, topology, consensus, transport, discovery, pairing, credential rotation, persistence, file sync, agent integration, testing, and delivery, with almost no filler prose. The compression is a real asset — it is also why the terminology collisions (F9) and the example-only wire fields (F5) matter more here than they would in a verbose document.

judgement_calls.note: RFC 2119 formalism (line 8 declares MUST/SHOULD/MAY normative, cites no RFC, and omits MUST NOT which is used five times). Fixing the declaration is a one-line edit worth making. Retro-fitting keywords across §2.1, §8.4, §10, and §11 is not — headings like "Required controls:", "Required behavior", and "Required unit/component subjects" are unambiguous in English, and adding ceremony to hundreds of bullets would fight the document's greatest strength. Reject the broader ask.
judgement_calls.title: Do not retro-fit RFC 2119 keywords across the whole document

judgement_calls.note: §12 has no property-based, model-based, or deterministic-simulation testing; risk 3 names Raft integration as a safety hazard. But the doc already gets much of that assurance by other means: cross-replica digest equality over a mixed-version cluster (834), snapshot-plus-replay equivalence (805), real SQLite and real three-voter Raft (811-812), boundary fault injection (829-832), clock and failpoint seams (794-797), continuous decode fuzzing (876-878). A property-based suite over reducers and canonical encoding is cheap and worth adding once §5/§6 payload schemas exist; a deterministic replay harness and a TLA+ model are real cost. Author's call — but if only one is added, make it the seeded deterministic replay, because a nightly chaos failure that recurs once in 200 runs without replay is unactionable.
judgement_calls.title: Property-based and deterministic-simulation testing: strengthening, not a gap

judgement_calls.note: V1 is large. Defensible cuts: drop `hlc` from the signed canonical event (line 344 already demotes it to display/diagnosis and 443 bars reducers from consulting clocks, so it buys nothing while carrying canonical-encoding, golden-fixture, and cross-platform-signature-stability obligations); ship 1 and 3 voters with 5 deferred, saving harness matrix width at 824. Reject the proposed swap of per-entry `leader_signature` for a periodic signed chain-head checkpoint — that changes the verification property (a single exported event stops being independently verifiable) rather than preserving it cheaply. `inbox/` is already marked optional and fully specified in two sentences; cutting it saves nothing. Regardless of which cuts are taken, §13 needs an explicit deferred-past-V1 list so scope is visible.
judgement_calls.title: V1 scope cuts

judgement_calls.note: Two postures are stated but not owned end-to-end. At-rest: line 713-715 says FDE is required without enumerating the new cleartext copies of repository content CodeComm creates outside the workspace (tmp/ bootstrap staging holding a full git bundle, conflicts/ resolution snapshots, sidecar staggered prior-version store at 601, state.db/WAL, consensus/). FDE cannot be enforced, but it can be detected and reported — add a first-run and `status`/`doctor` check plus the enumeration, and bound sidecar version retention (tmp hygiene is already covered at 582 and 709). Sidecar sandboxing: "where platform controls allow" (623-624) is an aspiration with no floor; naming a minimum per platform is worth doing but is legitimately a phase-5 decision.
judgement_calls.title: At-rest cleartext surface and the sidecar sandbox floor: own them or state the residual

judgement_calls.note: A subverted sidecar or agent process runs under the owner's account, which line 688 already places outside the V1 boundary, and 442-443 already concedes leases cannot stop a same-user process. So most of "compromised local process" is out of scope by construction. The one piece worth adding regardless of scope: per-member and per-agent-session admission control enforced in the reducer, so it is uniform across replicas — line 705's generic "file/request/queue/DB quotas" leaves one runaway agent (of 32 targeted) able to grow every replica's log and SQLite, which 12.3 scenario 18 tests only as an accidental disk-full condition.
judgement_calls.title: Compromised local process: mostly out of scope, but per-member quotas are not

judgement_calls.note: Whether an authorized pair carries one tunnel or one per direction (538-540) is unstated, but line 542 already mandates bounding stream count, byte rate, backpressure, and idle/lifetime, and whether the concurrent-tunnel bound is 28 or 56 changes no decision in the document. Lower priority than it looks. The adjacent 32-agent scope ambiguity is worth one clause: line 45 and benchmark axis 890 read session-wide, while the same-device regression at 864 requires 32-session responsiveness on one device — an 8x difference in per-daemon sizing for a number that is both a capacity commitment and a benchmark axis.
judgement_calls.title: Tunnel fan-out is a bounded-limit-without-a-number; the 32-agent scope is not

judgement_calls.note: §11 spends ~40 bullets on generic production-engineering practice while §6.2 defines the entire application domain in eight bullets. Moving the commodity parts of §11 to an engineering-standards appendix would make the body's proportions match where the risk actually is. Purely the author's preference — but if §11 stays in the body, its checkable subset needs to become gates (see should-fix), because "Production quality is a release criterion" (732) with nothing in 12.5 verifying it is satisfied by assertion at release time.
judgement_calls.title: Consider relocating generic §11 content to an appendix

must_fix.fix: Add a §6.0 "Domain model" with a typed schema per entity (fields, required/optional, size and cardinality bounds, relations, which fields are reducer-validated vs display-only), and a §5.4 event-kind registry enumerating every V1 `kind` with its `payload` schema, plus the `actor_type` and `capture_level` enums and whether `expected_entity_version` starts at 0 or 1 and applies to create-kind events. Specify the `context.{json,md}` schema, size bounds, and refresh trigger. Add the missing tables or state explicitly that they are projections over `events`: activity, peer acks, `credential_authorizations`, `control_file_proposals`/`approvals`, and membership/role/voter columns. Reference the registry from the MCP tool schemas (466-470) and the golden fixtures (816-820).
must_fix.problem: The entire application domain is eight bullets (429-437). There is not one field of a task, plan revision, memory record, or lease anywhere in the document: no title/description/size bounds, no priority or ordering, no dependency or parent relations, no acceptance criteria, no plan-to-task linkage, no memory record shape, no lease glob syntax or maximum duration. The event envelope types every metadata field but leaves `payload: {}` and `actions: []` opaque, and the V1 `kind` namespace is never enumerated even though §5.3 rejects unknown kinds deterministically. `context.{json,md}` (392, 425) — the primary agent-facing payload, exposed as `context.get` (467) and the read-only fallback (475) — has no specified content, schema, size bound, or refresh trigger. Ten wire fields (`credential_epoch`, `advertising_key_digest`, `advertisement_nonce`, `committed_membership_index`, `schema_version`, `entity_id`, `expected_entity_version`, `hlc`, `actor_type`, `previous_entry_hash`) appear exactly once each, inside JSON examples, with no type, bound, or enum. Two §2.1 goals — activity and acknowledgements — have no table in the 404-406 list, and `credential_authorizations` (the state every mTLS handshake validates against per 248) and control-file proposals/approvals have no persistence home at all.
must_fix.title: The product itself is unspecified: no domain model, no event-kind/payload registry, no generated-context schema, and named replicated state with no persistence home
must_fix.why_it_matters: Every reducer, projection table, MCP tool schema, TUI view, and golden fixture derives from these definitions, so nothing in §5-9, 12, or 13 can be built or tested. §12.2 requires unit coverage of "task/plan states" (803) and golden fixtures for canonical events (816) for entities that are never specified. The document's implementation-ready surface is inverted: the commodity layers (Raft usage, TLS, testing policy) are specified in depth and the differentiated product is a sketch — a reviewer learns how a task transition is committed but never what a task is, and therefore cannot judge whether CodeComm usefully coordinates agents at all.

must_fix.fix: Add a short crypto-primitives subsection to §4 (or expand ADR-003's required outputs) fixing exactly what the fixture gate needs, without expanding into a full cryptography spec: one named canonical encoding for signed bytes (e.g. RFC 8785 JCS over the §5.2 JSON, stating that the negotiated binary encoding at 296 is a transport wrapper only), the digest text encoding, the exact `device_id` derivation including hash and any truncation, the `previous_entry_hash` chain input, and a distinct ASCII domain-separation label per signature context (genesis, discovery, invite/credential key binding, origin proposal, leader consensus block, snapshot chain digest). Carry an algorithm identifier in the genesis policy so primitives are versioned. Leave suite selection to ADR-003 but name it as that ADR's required output with a phase-1 deadline.
must_fix.problem: No signature scheme, no hash function, no canonical serialization, and no per-context domain-separation label is named anywhere in the document. The only algorithm in the file is SHA-256 at line 572, for Git bundles. `device_id` is "Hash of long-lived device public key" (152) with no hash, encoding, or truncation, yet it is the identifier every authorization decision keys on. "Canonical" appears at 301, 380, 408, 509, 804, and 815 without ever being bound to a named encoding. `previous_entry_hash` (336) and the snapshot "chain digest" (373) have no stated chain input. The same enrolled identity key signs six structurally different objects (genesis record, discovery datagram, invite/credential key binding, origin proposal, leader consensus block, snapshot digest) with no domain tag.
must_fix.title: Canonical serialization, digest constructions, and domain separation are unspecified — the golden-fixture merge gate cannot be authored
must_fix.why_it_matters: Line 818 makes "cross-platform signature stability" and immutable golden fixtures over canonical events, batches, and signatures a merge gate. Those fixtures literally cannot be written from these definitions, so the gate is inert from day one and two OS builds of the same implementation may not agree on signed bytes. Suite selection is legitimately deferred to ADR-003; the canonical form and digest constructions are not, because they are prerequisites for phase 1's own CI. Absent domain separation is also the standard precondition for cross-protocol signature confusion, and it costs one line per context to close.

must_fix.fix: Decouple the hash chain from Raft ordering: drop leader-assigned term/log_index/previous_entry_hash from the signed proposal, let Raft own ordering, and have every replica derive the chain deterministically at apply over ACCEPTED events only — chain_n = H(domain_label || chain_{n-1} || canonical_accepted_event_n) with a stated hash and chain_version — recording observed (term, log_index) as unsigned local provenance. If a leader attestation is wanted, make it a separate periodic committed checkpoint signed over (term, applied_index, chain_digest) and proposed AFTER apply, which is expressible on standard library APIs. Add chain continuity to the step 5 recheck list (358-360) and name the trust anchor that verifies snapshot chain digests.
must_fix.problem: Lines 301-304 and step 3 (356) require the leader to assign term, log_index, and previous_entry_hash and sign them before proposing to Raft. Mainstream embedded Raft libraries — the ones line 727 mandates — do not expose the assigned index to the proposer pre-commit: hashicorp/raft's Apply/ApplyLog and etcd/raft's Propose both take a sealed payload and assign term and index internally, with no reservation API. The only workaround is serializing every proposal against LastIndex()+1, racing leader no-op and configuration entries and forbidding pipelining. Separately the chain's domain is undefined and self-contradictory: previous_entry_hash sits in the leader-signed block (336), but line 367 says rejected commands and Raft config entries consume indices so accepted-event indices have gaps — if the chain covers all Raft entries, a nonvoter receiving only accepted events in bounded signed batches (371) can never recompute it; if it covers accepted events only, the leader cannot compute it at propose time because acceptance is decided at apply (358-362). Chain continuity is also absent from the step 5 recheck list even though line 373 makes a snapshot chain digest load-bearing for joiners.
must_fix.title: The leader cannot pre-assign and sign (term, log_index, previous_entry_hash) on the mandated Raft libraries, and the hash chain's domain contradicts index gaps
must_fix.why_it_matters: This is the central integrity mechanism of the coordination plane and the concrete artifact behind the "No split-brain strong state" invariant. As written, an implementer must invent the chain domain, then discovers mid-phase-3 that the chosen library cannot supply pre-commit indices, and either forks the library, serializes all proposals (killing the 889 throughput benchmarks), or quietly drops the leader signature. Safety is not actually at risk — lines 88 and 303-305 make quorum commitment plus deterministic apply authoritative — so the fix is a localized redesign of one signed block, but it must happen before phase 3 rather than during it.

must_fix.fix: State the cardinality in §3's component table, e.g. "one `codecommd` per (user, session); clients discover running daemons via a per-user registry directory in the platform-standard config location; `codecomm` and the MCP adapter select one by `--session` or by workspace-root ancestry." Then reconcile the line 12/43 wording, define the socket/named-pipe naming and discovery scheme for local clients, scope the 2-8 device and 32-agent caps to a named unit, state the supported number of concurrent sessions per host with its multicast-advertiser, port, and resource implications, and confirm that one device identity key is shared across sessions while credential epochs are per-session.
must_fix.problem: Lines 12 and 43 specify one long-lived daemon per user. Line 654-655 specifies "a per-workspace OS lock [that] prevents two local daemons owning the same DB/sidecar home" — presupposing multiple daemons per user, one per workspace. Line 533 pins one Syncthing sidecar per session. All state lives under a workspace-relative `.codecomm/` (388-396) containing exactly one `session.json`, one `state.db`, and one `consensus/`, so the on-disk schema is single-session. The MCP process reaches the daemon "through a Unix socket or Windows named pipe" (456-459) — singular, with no addressing scheme for choosing among several. Nothing states whether a user may participate in two sessions or two workspaces concurrently, or whether that means two daemons, two sockets, two Raft clusters, two sidecars, and two multicast advertisers per interface.
must_fix.title: Daemon-to-session cardinality is contradictory: "per-user daemon" vs per-workspace lock, per-session sidecar, single-session on-disk layout, and one IPC socket
must_fix.why_it_matters: A developer working on two repositories concurrently is the ordinary case. The choice determines the process model, the IPC namespace and local discovery mechanism every client uses, the split between global identity and per-session state (401), listening-port and multicast-advertiser counts per host, resource budgets, and the meaning of the §14 targets. It is upstream of nearly every phase-2 task and is not resolvable from the text — which means the first three components built will each assume something different.

must_fix.fix: Add a §2.0 user model with a named primary persona and a named excluded one. If single-human: downgrade or cut two-sided SAS confirmation, self-grant prevention, and per-device role separation, and state that confidentiality among authorized members is explicitly not a goal. If multi-human: add a `user_id`/account identifier, bind application roles to users rather than devices, and add "authorized but distrusted collaborator" to the §10 threat list. File this as Open Question 0 with a decision deadline before phase 1 exits.
must_fix.problem: There is no user, person, or principal identity anywhere in the document. The identifier table (150-159) has device, session, workspace, agent-profile, agent-session, and event IDs — no human. Roles (§4.2) are granted to devices. Yet both models are silently assumed in different places. Multi-human: "Both users compare and confirm a short authentication string" (223-224) is not a ceremony if one person performs both halves; "cannot be self-granted" (183) is vacuous if one human owns every device; "workspace readability by authorized owner/editors" (686) is only a threat between distinct people; owner-approves-editor-proposals (179-181). Single-human: "per-user daemon" (12, 43), "cannot stop a same-user process from editing a path" (442), compromised local OS account out of scope (688), and the entire at-rest posture (713-715). §15 contains no question on this; OQ4 asks whether 2-8 devices is representative but never how many humans own them.
must_fix.title: The user model is never stated — one person with several devices, or several people? — and the doc silently assumes both
must_fix.why_it_matters: This single unresolved question determines whether the role model needs a user layer or is over-built; whether pairing needs two-sided out-of-band confirmation or that is theater; whether the audit log has a purpose; whether "cannot be self-granted", revocation, and the Byzantine-voter exclusion are meaningful controls or decoration; whether at-rest encryption is optional (my laptops) or mandatory (my teammate's disk holds my code); and whether conflict resolution UX is single-operator or negotiated. Roughly a third of the mechanisms in §4, §8.4, and §10 are priced for the multi-human case while the narrative voice is single-human.

must_fix.fix: Add a §6.3 "Ownership release and operator override": (a) claims release on agent-session end — the reducer returns the task to `ready` with a recorded reason when the committed agent-session-ended event applies; (b) an owner/editor force-release and reassign command that is a committed, audited, expected-version event; (c) `agent stop`, `task unclaim|reassign|cancel`, `lease release`, and `peer leave` in the CLI, with an explicit statement of which are deliberately absent from MCP so agents cannot self-authorize them; (d) failure-table rows for dead task owner, runaway agent, and abandoned worktree. Replace the two state chains (431, 498) with an edge list or table naming terminal states, return edges out of `blocked` and `disconnected`, release from `claimed`, and the expired-owner outcome, and state that `sync_blocked` is an orthogonal flag gating `-> done` rather than a member of the state enum.
must_fix.problem: Line 496 says agent-session expiry "ends the session, releases leases, and forbids ID reuse" — leases are released, task claims are not. Task ownership is `(device_id, agent_session_id)` (432) and `agent_session_id` is never reused (156, 496), so a task in `claimed`/`in_progress`/`blocked` whose owning agent session ended is permanently owned by an identity that can never return, and the compare-and-set reducer will reject transitions proposed by anyone else. The whole mutation surface is one-directional: MCP has `task.list/claim/update`, `lease.acquire/renew`, `plan.get/propose`, `memory.append`, `activity.append` — no unclaim, reassign, lease.release, memory tombstone, or plan rollback; the CLI has `task add|claim|start|block|done` with no `agent stop`, `task unclaim|reassign|cancel`, `lease release`, or voluntary departure (only `peer revoke`). The failure table (657-676) covers 21 infrastructure failures and zero human-intervention scenarios. Separately, lines 431 and 498 give task and agent states as ordered chains rather than edge sets, so the transitions reducers must validate deterministically (360) and unit tests must cover (804) are never enumerated.
must_fix.title: No ownership release or operator override: a task claimed by a dead agent session is permanently unworkable, and no verb can release it
must_fix.why_it_matters: This is a liveness defect reachable by the most common event in the system — an agent process exiting. Every affected task becomes permanently unworkable with no documented remedy, and because completion is additionally blocked by unresolved conflicts (600) the same dead end applies to `sync_blocked` work. More broadly, a coordination tool for autonomous agents whose only human verbs are "start more work" is missing the half of the interface operators use most: stop, take back, redo, hand off. Risk 7 (973-974) already concedes agents may ignore the workflow, which makes override the required response, not an optional one.

must_fix.fix: Add a normative subsection to §5.3: (a) a per-command minimum-apply-version or feature gate, with the rule that a replica which cannot deterministically apply a committed entry halts and refuses to advance its applied index rather than substituting a local rejection, surfaced as a blocker state in the TUI/CLI; (b) the supported version-skew window (e.g. N-1) and the requirement that new reducer semantics ship dark and activate only via a committed capability-enable entry; (c) a normative invariant in §6.2 that reducer behavior for an existing (kind, schema_version) MUST NOT change, added to line 783's non-mergeable list. Define the projection digest in §12.3 as an ordered fold over a named set of tables, rows canonically encoded with explicit field order and sorted by primary key, with a `digest_version` and named hash, and define "eligible" as same digest_version and schema_version.
must_fix.problem: Two linked gaps. (1) No section states what a replica does when it encounters a committed Raft entry it cannot deterministically apply — a kind, field, or reducer branch it does not implement. Line 292-294's "Unknown required capabilities fail closed" is scoped to wire messages in §5.1 and does not cover an already-committed entry. Nor is there any stated version-skew window, or any rule freezing reducer semantics per schema version: a v1.1 daemon that "fixes" a transition rule accepts at index N what a v1.0 replica stored as a structured rejection (362), diverging both permanently while both believe they are deterministic. (2) "Projection digest" — the harness pass/fail criterion at 834-836 — appears exactly once in the document, with no covered tables, row ordering, per-row encoding, hash, digest versioning, or definition of "eligible". SQLite page hashes are nondeterministic across vacuum and rowid reuse, and unordered SELECT is not stable, so implementers will guess differently.
must_fix.title: No runtime rule for a committed entry a replica cannot apply, no version-skew policy, no frozen reducer semantics, and "projection digest" is undefined
must_fix.why_it_matters: This is the one class of bug that silently destroys the correctness story the whole design rests on, and it triggers on the first real upgrade because nothing stops a user from updating one laptop. It is also the only place the doc's own divergence detector could catch it — and that detector (834) is undefined, so it cannot be implemented. The compensating controls are real but test-time only: line 783 gates reducer changes on compatibility coverage and 848 replicates across versions in the harness. There is no production-time detection, and the recovery path is line 143's owner-approved new trust epoch, the heaviest procedure in the document. This constrains how every future behavior change ships, so it must be settled before the first reducer is written.

must_fix.fix: Add a subsection to §2.2 or §4.3 covering endpoint churn: make local address change an observable event that triggers re-advertisement and peer reconnect; state whether endpoint hints are committed state or gossip, with a TTL and refresh rule; give the multicast interval a value and make advertisement MUST on selected interfaces; specify reconnect backoff and tunnel re-establishment. Add failure-table rows for host suspend/resume, interface change, and address change, and state the required behavior for waking with an expired credential epoch while quorum is unreachable. Justify the 30-minute epoch numerically, make it a committed genesis-policy value with a stated default and range, and require impending expiry to surface as a distinct TUI/CLI state with a countdown, separate from the post-hoc `expired` state at line 632.
must_fix.problem: §2.2 covers which networks work but never a network changing. Peer endpoints come from committed roster hints (276) and multicast, and line 207 says the source address is only a hint — but nothing specifies how a peer's address is updated when it changes, whether address changes are committed events, how a device re-establishes direct connections and Syncthing tunnels after DHCP renewal, Wi-Fi-to-Ethernet switch, VPN reconnect, or suspend/resume, or how long stale hints are retried before falling back to multicast. Sleep/wake appears exactly once in the document, as a native test-matrix item (885), with no requirement to test against. Multicast advertisement is MAY (188) at a jittered but unnumbered interval, so it is not a reliable re-discovery mechanism, and the manual-endpoint fallback (211) is a human action. The failure table has no row for address change, host suspend, or interface disappearance. The 30-minute credential epoch is never justified numerically, is not stated to be a configurable committed policy value, and has no pre-expiry warning.
must_fix.title: Endpoint churn, suspend/resume, and address change have no treatment, and they interact directly with the 30-minute credential epoch
must_fix.why_it_matters: For a local-first tool on developer laptops, address change and suspend/resume are the dominant availability events — far more frequent than voter loss or DB corruption, both of which get dedicated failure rows. Unhandled, they produce exactly the outcome the design most wants to avoid: peers that are physically reachable but stay disconnected until a human re-enters an endpoint, stalled tunnels, and elections triggered by a sleeping voter. The interaction is the sharp part: a laptop closed for 40 minutes wakes with expired credentials and, if quorum is elsewhere and unreachable, into the renewal-only path with no session data — and neither §4.5 nor §9 mentions suspend at all.

ordered_edits: 1. Add §2.0 User model (one paragraph): named primary persona, named excluded persona, and whether authorized-member confidentiality is a goal. File as Open Question 0, decision due before phase 1 exits. Everything below depends on the answer.

2. Fix cardinality in §3's component table: daemon-per-(user, session), local daemon registry and client selection rule, socket/named-pipe naming, concurrent sessions per host, and the unit the 2-8 device and 32-agent caps are scoped to. Reconcile lines 12/43 with 654-655 and 533.

3. Add §6.0 Domain model: typed schema per entity (task, plan revision, memory record, lease) with fields, bounds, relations, and reducer-validated vs display-only marking. This is the single largest missing artifact and unblocks §5.4, the MCP schemas, the TUI, and every fixture.

4. Add §5.4 Event-kind registry: every V1 `kind` with its `payload` schema, plus `actor_type`/`capture_level` enums and the `expected_entity_version` base and create-event rule. Add a field table for the ten example-only wire fields.

5. Add §4.0 Crypto primitives: canonical encoding for signed bytes (e.g. RFC 8785 JCS over §5.2 JSON, with 296's binary encoding declared a transport wrapper), digest text encoding, exact `device_id` derivation, `previous_entry_hash` chain input, and one domain-separation label per signature context. Name suite selection as ADR-003's required phase-1 output.

6. Rewrite the §5.2 `consensus` block and §5.3 step 3: drop leader pre-assignment of term/log_index/previous_entry_hash from the signed proposal; derive the chain deterministically at apply over accepted events only; record observed (term, log_index) as unsigned provenance; optionally add a post-apply signed checkpoint over (term, applied_index, chain_digest). all_findings.problem: 4.5 (240-255) does not say which party assigns `issue_time`/`expiry` or state the corresponding reducer checks, and the discovery field `credential_epoch` (197) reads session-global while 4.5 describes a per-device epoch binding.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Line 254-255 makes credential expiry the *only* bound on a stale/partitioned or later-revoked peer ("bounding stale access by the current credential expiry"), and line 694 lists "bounded stale partition lifetime" as a required control. If the requester supplies `expiry`, a malicious-but-authorized editor — or a compromised agent/daemon on any member device — proposes `expiry = now + 10 years`, quorum commits it because no rule rejects it, and every peer then accepts that certificate per step 6. Revocation of that device becomes unenforceable against any peer that later partitions with it, and the entire rotation design collapses to a static long-lived credential. Preconditions are only "one authorized member is malicious or compromised", which section 10 already assumes (685: "lost/compromised former members") and which is *not* excluded by the Byzantine-voter non-goal at 77 (that non-goal is about consensus safety, not about self-granted authorization scope).
all_findings.recommendation: Add one clause to 4.5: the leader assigns `issue_time`, and the deterministic reducer rejects authorizations whose lifetime exceeds the genesis-policy epoch length plus overlap, whose epoch is not the successor of the device's last committed epoch, or whose key digest was previously authorized. State whether `epoch` is per-device or session-global and make 197 consistent. Extend the 12.2 credential-epoch bullet with over-long-expiry, epoch-rollback, and digest-reuse cases.
all_findings.verifier_note: The unbounded-lifetime exploit is not supported as written. Line 238 fixes the policy ("a fresh TLS key authenticates each 30-minute epoch"), 250-252 fix the renew-early and 2-minute overlap numbers, 168 puts "protocol policy" in the immutable genesis record, and 5.3 step 5 (358-360) already requires every state machine to deterministically recheck "membership, signatures, actor binding, authorization, schema, sequence, transition, and expected version against prior committed state" — an implementer validating "authorization" against committed policy is the natural reading, not one that accepts requester-supplied expiry. 254-255 asserts the bound ("bounding stale access by the current credential expiry") and 97 makes it an invariant ("No insecure minority renewal"). The attacker model also requires a malicious authorized member, which 76 excludes as a non-goal in spirit ("Byzantine tolerance against malicious authorized voters"). What survives is a genuine but narrow specification gap: the doc never says explicitly that the leader/reducer assigns and clamps issue_time/expiry, never states per-device epoch monotonicity or digest-nonreuse as a reducer check (251's "never reuse keys" is guidance), and 197's session-global-looking `credential_epoch` vs 4.5's per-device binding is ambiguous. That is a minor tightening, not a blocker.

all_findings.title: Signature algorithms, hash functions, canonical encoding, and domain separation are entirely unspecified across six distinct signing contexts
all_findings.lines: 150 (`device_id` = "Hash of long-lived device public key"), 168-170 (genesis record), 203 (discovery `signature`), 222 ("signed genesis digest"), 242 (identity signs key binding), 301-306 and 328-343 (origin + leader signatures), 373-374 (snapshot chain digest), 408 ("canonical structured encoding")
all_findings.problem: No signature scheme, hash function, `device_id` construction, or canonical serialization is named anywhere, and no per-context domain-separation label is required for the several distinct objects the enrolled identity key signs (168, 222, 203, 242, 301-306, 373).
all_findings.why_it_matters: Two concrete consequences. (a) Cross-protocol signature confusion: with no domain tag and no fixed canonical encoding, an attacker who can get an honest member to sign one object type looks for a byte sequence that also parses as another — e.g. a signed discovery datagram or an origin event proposal whose canonical bytes are accepted as a credential key binding (242) or as a leader `consensus` block (331-338). The pre-pairing discovery signer (209) is the cheapest oracle since any LAN host can solicit datagrams. (b) Implementability: 12.2 requires "cross-platform signature stability" golden fixtures (816-818) and "immutable golden fixtures cover canonical events/batches/signatures" — those fixtures cannot be authored at all without a byte-level canonical form. The same applies to `device_id`, which is a security identifier used for authorization decisions and cannot be implemented from "Hash of long-lived device public key".
all_findings.recommendation: Add a short crypto-primitives subsection to section 4 naming the signature scheme and hash, giving `device_id` an exact construction (including truncation and encoding), naming the canonical serialization that 301/408 refer to, requiring a distinct ASCII domain label per signature context, and carrying an algorithm identifier in the genesis policy so primitives are versioned. This is a prerequisite for the golden fixtures at 815-818.
all_findings.verifier_note: The factual core checks out: SHA-256 appears only at 572 for Git bundles; no signature scheme, no hash for `device_id`/`previous_entry_hash`/chain digest, and no named canonical serialization exist anywhere, while 301 and 408 reference "canonical" forms and 815 requires immutable golden fixtures over "canonical events/batches/signatures" plus cross-platform signature stability — those fixtures genuinely cannot be authored without a byte-level form. But the framing is overstated. "Blocker" implies the design cannot work; it can — this is a decision deferred to the ADR/spike stage the doc explicitly schedules (768 "Require focused review for crypto, identity/auth...", 914 security/dependency spikes, 730 "Do not implement cryptography"). The cross-protocol signature-confusion exploit is speculative: the signed objects carry distinguishing typed fields (307-319 shows schema_version/event_id/session_id/workspace_id), and no oracle is demonstrated — 209 explicitly says the pre-pairing discovery signature is "informational", so it is not an authorization oracle.

all_findings.title: Short authentication string derivation is unspecified — no length/entropy floor, no transcript definition, no abort semantics
all_findings.problem: 4.4 step 6 does not define the SAS transcript inputs, output length/alphabet, retry policy, or the requirement to void the invite on mismatch, and the doc never states what the SAS adds beyond the fingerprint pinning at 220-221.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The SAS is one of the two named pairing controls in the required-controls list (692-693: "two-sided confirmation"). If it is 6 decimal digits with retry-on-mismatch, an attacker gets a 1-in-10^6 guess per attempt with unbounded attempts, which is a break rather than a control. If the transcript is not bound to the TLS channel and to both identity public keys, the SAS confirms nothing an attacker cannot also produce. The doc also never says *what threat* the SAS defends against given that step 3 already pins the inviter fingerprint out of band — without that rationale an implementer may downgrade or drop it as redundant, losing the protection against a leaked/phished invite bundle being redeemed by the wrong joiner (the inviter's human is the only party who can catch that).
all_findings.recommendation: Specify SAS = fixed-length rendering of KDF(domain label, transcript or TLS exporter, both identity public keys, session_id, genesis digest) with a stated minimum entropy, exactly one comparison attempt, and mandatory invite invalidation on mismatch or timeout. Add one clause stating what it protects against that pinning does not (redeemed-by-wrong-joiner after invite disclosure).
all_findings.verifier_note: The gap is real — 223-224 is the only SAS text and gives no KDF, transcript definition, length, or mismatch semantics — but the impact argument misreads the flow. The SAS is compared over a channel that step 3 has already pinned to the inviter identity out of band and step 4 has already authenticated ("TLS verifies the inviter's long-lived identity and genesis binding", 221), and step 5 requires the invite-secret proof. A 6-digit SAS in that position is not "a 1-in-10^6 guess per attempt" break, because the attacker must already defeat pinned mTLS and the 128-bit invite secret; 233's prohibition is specifically on "Unverified TLS plus a six-digit password", which is not this configuration. 693 also lists rate limits among required controls. The residual defect is under-specification of the SAS derivation and abort behavior, not a breakable control.

all_findings.title: Invite-secret proof mechanism is not specified, and invite consumption durability/scope is undefined
all_findings.problem: 4.4 does not state the form of the invite-secret proof, nor where one-use consumption is recorded and whether it is durable before the response is sent; there is also no outstanding-invite cap and no invite list/revoke surface.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Three separate consequences. (a) A bearer presentation puts a 128-bit credential into an HTTP request body on the responder, where it can land in structured request logs, problem responses (293), or a crash report — the doc bans secrets in argv/env/URL/log at 230-231 for *input* but does not extend that ban to the server-side handling of the received proof; 12.4 tests "invite leakage" (868) with no design rule to test against. (b) Without channel binding, a proof observed or replayed on one connection can be presented on another; combined with an undefined "one-use" enforcement point this admits concurrent redemption. (c) If consumption is only local and non-durable, an inviter crash or restart between step 5 and step 9 (a case 12.3 explicitly exercises: "leader/voter/peer crashes", 829) leaves the invite live for a second redemption; if consumption *is* committed, the doc must say so because it makes pairing require quorum, which contradicts "An owner on any healthy member creates" (217) in a minority partition.
all_findings.recommendation: Name the proof (HMAC/PAKE over the transcript rather than bearer presentation) and bind it to the step-4 channel. State that one-use consumption is durable before the response and define the behavior if the inviter restarts mid-pairing (fail closed). Add an outstanding-invite cap and a `codecomm invite list|revoke` command.
all_findings.verifier_note: Sub-claims (a) and (b) do not hold. Step 5 says the joiner "proves" the secret, and secret hygiene is not limited to input: 752 requires redacting secret types and excludes secrets from URLs/argv/logs generally, 706 requires "Redaction before persistence/replication" and rate-limited local logs, 837 adds "artifact scans for invite/credential leakage", and 753 requires erasing mutable buffers — so the server-side-logging story is already covered. Channel-binding replay is also weak because the proof travels inside TLS already authenticated against the pinned inviter identity (220-221), so a second connection would have to be the inviter. What survives is (c): 228's "The invite is consumed" never says where consumption state lives or that it is durable before the response, which matters against the crash cases at 829, plus the absence of any invite cap or `invite list|revoke` surface in the CLI (635-651) or REST table (273-291).

all_findings.title: Renewal-only handshake is a pre-auth surface with no specified freshness challenge or responder-freshness requirement
all_findings.problem: 257-259 does not specify the renewal-handshake proof construction (server nonce, bound fields, channel binding), does not give the responder an applied-index staleness floor before forwarding, and `POST /v1/credentials/renew` (280) does not distinguish the pre-auth expired-member path from the authenticated one.
all_findings.why_it_matters: (a) With no freshness challenge, a captured renewal proof is replayable indefinitely — the attacker needs only to have observed one renewal from a device whose long-lived key was later compromised or whose device was revoked. (b) A lagging or partitioned responder that has not yet applied the revocation entry will accept and forward renewal requests from a revoked device; the leader will reject them, so trust is not broken, but this is an unauthenticated-to-us party driving leader and Raft work, i.e. a quorum-wide DoS amplification from a pre-auth endpoint. (c) This is the endpoint an attacker who has extracted a long-lived identity key (the one asset the doc keeps in the OS credential store, 165) attacks first, and it is the one endpoint that must serve parties with no valid transport credential. `POST /v1/credentials/renew` (280) does not distinguish the authenticated-renewal path from the expired-member path, so the rate limits and role checks that apply to it are ambiguous.
all_findings.recommendation: Specify: responder issues a nonce; requester signs (domain label, nonce, session_id, device_id, epoch, new key digest, channel binding); responder verifies against committed membership and revocation, refuses to proposeanything before the signature verifies, and rejects if its applied index is staler than a stated bound. Annotate the pre-auth-reachable endpoint separately in the REST table and add a 12.4 case for renewal by a revoked device against a lagging responder.
all_findings.verifier_note: The replay harm is not established: a captured renewal request carries a key digest the attacker does not hold the private key for, so replaying it authorizes nothing useful; obtaining a credential still requires signing a fresh binding with the long-lived key (241). The DoS argument is also blunted — 257 already says the handshake is "rate-limited", 258-259 says the requester "receives no session data or other API access until quorum commits a new authorization", 253 closes sessions on revocation observation, 741-743 requires bounded queues and backpressure, and 869 already tests "expired/revoked/stale credentials". What remains is that the proof's construction (server nonce, channel binding, staleness floor on the responder's applied index, comparable to the correct requirement at 247-248) is unspecified, and that 280 does not distinguish the pre-auth expired-member path from the authenticated renewal path.

all_findings.title: "Long-lived private keys MUST stay in the OS credential store" has no specified fallback for the common headless-Linux case
all_findings.problem: 165 makes OS-credential-store residency a MUST and 708 enumerates the three providers, but the doc never states the daemon's behavior when no provider is available or unlocked (headless Linux, no D-Bus session, locked keyring at unattended boot).
all_findings.why_it_matters: A MUST with no achievable path on a supported platform gets silently downgraded during implementation — the predictable outcome is a mode-0600 file under the config dir, which is a materially different security posture, is not disclosed anywhere in section 10, and directly undermines SEC-5 (the long-lived key is the sole credential the renewal-only handshake accepts). 11 already forbids exactly this pattern: "do not fake parity by weakening the hardest platform" (772-773) and "No critical path ships with ... platform-disabled security/durability" (770-771). The doc must resolve it rather than leaving it to the implementer.
all_findings.recommendation: Resolve it in one clause or list it in section 15: either refuse to start with a named operator remedy, or specify the fallback (path/mode, passphrase-wrapped with a named KDF, unattended-start behavior, degraded-posture indicator in `status`) plus an assumption line in section 10. Add the no-keyring headless case to the native matrix at 881-885.
all_findings.verifier_note: The external facts are right (no Secret Service without a session bus; Linux is a V1 platform at 17; `systemd --user` at 653; reboot/join tested at 905) and no fallback or failure behavior is stated. But "no achievable path on a supported platform" overstates it: Secret Service is achievable on the developer desktops this design targets, headless Linux is nowhere stated as a V1 target, and the doc already forbids the predicted silent downgrade — 770-771 bans "platform-disabled security/durability" on a critical path and 772-773 bans faking parity by weakening the hardest platform, so an implementer dropping to a mode-0600 file would be violating an explicit release criterion rather than filling a vacuum. This is an unresolved platform decision of the kind section 15 exists for, not a major security defect.

all_findings.title: Discovery replay protection has no receiver-side rules, no inbound rate limit, and the packet leaks cluster metadata the doc does not acknowledge
all_findings.problem: 4.3 declares `advertisement_nonce` and `expires_at` (201-202) without any receiver-side acceptance rules (nonce cache scope/bound/TTL, future horizon, clock-skew allowance, behavior with no trusted clock given link-local operation at 70), and the omission list at 207-208 does not acknowledge that `session_id`, `credential_epoch`, `committed_membership_index`, and `pairing_open` are still broadcast.
all_findings.why_it_matters: (a) Without a defined nonce cache and skew bound, "replay protection" is unimplementable and untestable — 12.4 lists "spoofed discovery" tests (868) and continuous discovery fuzzing (876) with no acceptance rule; a naive implementation with an unbounded nonce set is itself a memory-exhaustion target from a single unauthenticated LAN host. (b) An unauthenticated multicast sender on a hostile LAN — the doc's stated assumption (684) — floods 1,200-byte signed-looking datagrams and consumes CPU on every daemon on the segment; this is the only pre-auth network surface reachable without any secret. (c) `pairing_open` in particular is a targeting oracle that raises the value of a guessing/DoS attack on the pairing endpoint, and `session_id` disclosure lets a passive observer track the same collaboration as it moves between networks. The omission list at 207-208 reads as a completed privacy analysis, which makes these residual leaks easy to miss.
all_findings.recommendation: State the receiver rules: bounded nonce cache keyed per source with a TTL tied to the advertisement interval, a maximum accepted `expires_at` horizon with a named skew allowance and a defined no-trusted-clock behavior, and cheap checks before any signature work. Either drop `pairing_open`/`committed_membership_index` or add one sentence accepting the residual metadata disclosure.
all_findings.verifier_note: Sub-claim (a) is the real one: `advertisement_nonce` and `expires_at` are declared at 201-202 with no receiver-side cache scope, eviction, horizon, or skew rule anywhere, while 693 asserts "replay/idempotency protection" and 868/876 test and fuzz spoofed discovery — so the acceptance rule is genuinely missing. Sub-claim (b) is largely covered: 189 caps size below 1,200 bytes with TTL 1, 209 states the pre-pairing signature is only "informational" (so no mandatory pre-pairing verification cost), 705 requires request/queue quotas, and 741-743 require bounded queues and backpressure. Sub-claim (c) is accurate but small — the packet does carry `session_id`, `credential_epoch`, `committed_membership_index`, and `pairing_open`, and 207-208 reads as a completed omission list — but this is disclosed-metadata hygiene on a link-local, TTL-1 datagram, not a security break.

all_findings.title: Threat model omits three adversary classes the architecture is specifically exposed to: compromised sidecar, compromised agent process, and denial of service by an authorized member
all_findings.problem: No per-member or per-agent-session admission control or fairness rule is specified for `POST /v1/events` and lease/task claims, so the generic quotas at 705 leave one runaway or subverted authorized editor able to grow every replica's log and SQLite; the sidecar sandbox floor is also left as "where platform controls allow" (623-624).
all_findings.why_it_matters: These three are the highest-likelihood post-pairing adversaries in a design whose whole premise is running untrusted-output coding agents against a shared workspace. Their absence has concrete design consequences rather than being merely documentary: no per-member/per-agent rate limit or quota is specified anywhere, so an implementer will build none, and a single compromised or merely runaway agent instance (the doc targets 32 concurrent instances, 46) can exhaust every peer's disk — which 12.3 scenario 18 tests ("Exhaust Raft/SQLite disk") only as an accidental condition. Similarly, without a stated sidecar-compromise posture the sidecar's platform sandboxing ("bounded resources and access ... where platform controls allow", 623-624) stays a best-effort aspiration with no requirement behind it.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a committed per-member/per-agent rate-and-quota rule enforced in the reducer so it is uniform across replicas, and name a minimum sidecar sandbox per platform rather than a conditional. If compromised local processes remain out of scope, say so explicitly next to 688 rather than relying on the "local OS account" wording.
all_findings.verifier_note: Two of the three classes are already inside the doc's stated boundary or exclusions. A subverted sidecar or agent process runs under the owner's account, which 688 explicitly places outside the V1 boundary ("A compromised local OS account ... outside the V1 boundary"); 442-443 already concedes leases "cannot stop a same-user process from editing a path"; risk 1 concedes that provenance and control paths "cannot replace sandbox and approvals" for agent influence; 288 already labels sidecar status "Sanitized"; 533 and 623-624 give the sidecar an unprivileged pinned identity with bounded resources; 76 excludes Byzantine authorized voters. Resource abuse is partly covered by 705 ("file/request/queue/DB quotas"), 741-743, and the disk-exhaustion scenario at 12.3 #18. The narrow surviving point is that no per-member or per-agent-session admission control is specified anywhere, and that the reducer is the only place it would be uniform across replicas.

all_findings.title: Loopback listeners are treated as an authorization boundary for the sync connector and sidecar, while local IPC correctly uses peer-UID/ACL checks
all_findings.lines: 534-538 (sidecar API/listener), 289 and 538 (per-pair local connector), contrast 456-459 and 698
all_findings.problem: 538's per-pair local CodeComm connector ports have no stated local access control, unlike MCP/IPC which specifies peer-UID/socket-mode/named-pipe ACL (456-459, 698), and 688 does not clearly place same-host non-owner accounts outside the V1 boundary.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A second unprivileged local user connects to a per-pair connector port and gets a path into the authenticated cross-device tunnel (bounded in practice by Syncthing's own device TLS inside the tunnel, which is why this is minor rather than major), and can also probe/DoS the sidecar management API port and the CodeComm HTTPS port. 12.4 tests "network reachability of local APIs" (870-871) — i.e. that they are not remotely reachable — but not local cross-account reachability, so the gap would not be caught.
all_findings.recommendation: Prefer Unix sockets or named pipes with owner-only mode/ACL for the per-pair connectors, or require a per-connection secret / peer-credential check where a loopback TCP port is unavoidable; alternatively state in 688 that same-host non-owner accounts are out of scope. Extend the 12.4 local-API case (870-871) to assert non-owner local accounts are refused.
all_findings.verifier_note: The asymmetry is real for the per-pair connectors — 538 gives them no stated authentication — and 688's "compromised local OS account" wording does not clearly cover a different unprivileged user on the same host, so the gap is genuine and correctly rated minor. But the sidecar half is overstated: 535-536 protects the management API with "a random owner-protected key and pinned local certificate", so it is not relying on loopback binding as its authorization boundary, and 543 keeps Syncthing's own device TLS inside the tunnel, so a rogue local process reaching a connector cannot impersonate a device.

all_findings.title: No cryptographic primitives or canonical serialization named — signing/verification cannot be implemented
all_findings.problem: The signed-data layer is underspecified where it feeds a merge gate. No canonical serialization is named for the bytes covered by the origin and leader signatures (342-343), so 'canonical' at 301, 380, 408, 804, and 815 carries several unrelated meanings; `device_id` (152) is 'hash of long-lived device public key' with no hash, encoding, or truncation; and `previous_entry_hash` (336) and the snapshot 'chain digest' (373) have no stated chain input. Line 818 requires golden fixtures for 'cross-platform signature stability' and canonical events, which cannot be authored from these definitions. Algorithm/suite choice itself is legitimately deferred to the phase-1 ADRs (913) and ADR-003 (984).
all_findings.why_it_matters: Two independent implementations, or even one implementation across two OSes, cannot produce byte-identical signed input. §12.2 line 818 makes "cross-platform signature stability" and golden signature fixtures a merge gate — those fixtures literally cannot be authored from this document. This is also the security core: every invariant at lines 88-97 and every control at lines 692-696 reduces to "the signature verified".
all_findings.recommendation: Do not expand this into a full cryptography specification; the doc intentionally defers suite choice to phase-1 ADRs. Add only what the golden-fixture gate at 815-819 requires: one named canonical encoding for signed bytes (e.g. RFC 8785 JCS over the §5.2 JSON, stating that the negotiated binary encoding at 296 is a transport wrapper only), the digest text encoding (base64url unpadded, already implied), the `device_id` derivation including any truncation, and the `previous_entry_hash` chain input. Note in §13 phase 1 or ADR-003 that the signature suite, hash function, and SPAKE2+ ciphersuite/SAS derivation are that ADR's required outputs.
all_findings.verifier_note: The grep-verified core is real: the only algorithm named anywhere is SHA-256 at line 572 (Git bundle digest), plus TLS 1.3 (23, 260) and SPAKE2+ (232); no signature suite, no hash for `device_id` (152), and 'canonical' (301, 380, 408, 509, 804, 815) is never bound to a named encoding, while line 818 makes cross-platform signature stability a golden-fixture merge gate. External facts asserted are correct (RFC 9383 = SPAKE2+, RFC 8785 = JCS). But 'blocker / cannot be implemented' is inflated: line 81 and line 730 deliberately delegate all primitives to reviewed libraries, and §13 phase 1 (913-916) makes 'threat model/ADRs' plus 'Raft/library/store review' and 'mTLS pairing, revocation, rotation' the first deliverable, with ADR-003 (984) still an open backlog item. The suite selection is an acknowledged pending ADR, not a design that cannot work. The genuinely sharp sub-point is narrower than the title: the canonical signed-bytes encoding and the `device_id`/`previous_entry_hash` digest constructions must be fixed before the line 815-819 fixtures can be authored.

all_findings.title: Line 139 is factually wrong given line 135: a one-voter two-device session does survive one failure
all_findings.problem: Line 139 says 'No two-device configuration can preserve strict writes after either device fails', but line 135 explicitly permits a one-voter configuration, where quorum is 1 and loss of the nonvoter leaves strong writes available. The sentence is only true of a two-voter configuration. Separately, the doc never states the default voter count for a given device count, nor when a joining device is promoted to voter.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the single most load-bearing availability claim in the document — it is what justifies "a third independent voting device is required" (140) and it appears in the risk register. An implementer who reads 135 and builds a 1-voter default ships a system where a 2-device session silently has a single point of failure for strong state and, worse, where the lone voter can commit membership and credential changes with no second party. An implementer who reads 139 and builds a 2-voter default ships a system that deadlocks on any single laptop closing its lid.
all_findings.recommendation: Reword 139 to 'No two-voter configuration can preserve strong writes after either voter fails, and a one-voter configuration places all strong state on a single device'. Also replace 'strict' with 'strong' there (see F9). Add one sentence to §3 giving the default voter count per device count and stating who proposes promotion on admission.
all_findings.verifier_note: The literal inconsistency is real: line 135 permits a one-voter session, in which quorum is 1, so a two-device session losing the nonvoter keeps strong writes — making line 139's 'after either device fails' inaccurate. But 'blocker' is wrong on both prongs. The substantive availability claim the doc is making is stated correctly three other times: line 61 ('automatic strong-state failover requires three voters'), line 136 ('three voters: recommended; tolerates one unavailable voter'), and line 940. No implementer reading 61+135-137 concludes anything other than 'you need three voters for fault-tolerant strong writes'. The compounding claims are also weaker than stated: line 183 forbids self-granted role/voter changes, and the CLI at 635 is explicitly labelled 'Representative', so its lack of a voter verb is not a gap — voter change is an owner capability at 181, a required behavior at 675, and a tested scenario at 857. The default voter count per device count and the promotion trigger are genuinely unstated.

all_findings.title: Task and agent state machines are written as linear chains that omit every real edge; no CLI verb can leave `blocked`, and `sync_blocked` is unclassified
all_findings.problem: Lines 431 and 498 list task and agent states as a single ordered chain rather than an edge set, so the transitions that reducers must validate deterministically (360) and that unit tests must cover (804) are not enumerated — notably the return edges out of `blocked` and `disconnected` (the latter required by the resume capability at 494-496), release from `claimed`, and the state of a task whose owning agent session expired. Whether `sync_blocked` (598) is a state or an orthogonal completion blocker is inferable from line 600 but not stated.
all_findings.why_it_matters: These transitions are enforced deterministically on every replica (line 360, "transition" is a listed recheck) and are a required unit-test subject (line 804). An ambiguous graph means two replicas can disagree on validity, which is a consensus safety bug, not a UI bug. It is also the highest-probability place for an implementer to guess wrong.
all_findings.recommendation: Replace the two chains with a short edge list or table naming terminal states, return edges, and the expired-owner outcome, and state in one clause that `sync_blocked` is an orthogonal flag that gates `-> done` rather than a member of the state enum.
all_findings.verifier_note: Both prongs of the framing fail on inspection. Reading `backlog -> ready -> claimed -> in_progress -> blocked -> done` (431) and `starting -> idle -> ... -> ended` (498) as literal graphs that force every task through `blocked` is an uncharitable reading of obvious shorthand for a state inventory in typical order; a competent implementer would not be misled. The CLI complaint is refuted outright by line 635, which labels the listing 'Representative' — grep confirming zero hits for 'unblock' proves nothing about the design. The 'consensus safety bug' escalation is unsupported: replicas run one binary, and 848 already tests current/previous-version replication. What survives is a real but modest completeness gap: line 360 makes 'transition' a deterministic recheck and 804 makes 'task/plan states' a required unit-test subject, yet the legal edge set is never enumerated, and the state of a task whose owning agent session expired (495-496, 661) is unstated. `sync_blocked` at 598-600 reads clearly as an orthogonal completion blocker ('scoped tasks cannot complete unresolved'), and 673 is about control-file proposals, not task state.

all_findings.title: Eleven wire fields exist only inside the JSON examples — never defined, typed, or bounded — and timestamp formats disagree
all_findings.problem: Ten wire fields (`credential_epoch`, `advertising_key_digest`, `advertisement_nonce`, `committed_membership_index`, `schema_version`, `entity_id`, `expected_entity_version`, `hlc`, `actor_type`, `previous_entry_hash`) appear only inside the §4.3 and §5.2 JSON examples, with no type, bound, or enum anywhere and no row in the §4.1 table. The reducer-relevant ones are the gap that matters: the V1 `kind` namespace is never enumerated even though §5.3 rejects unknown kinds deterministically, `actor_type` and `capture_level` have no enums, `expected_entity_version` has no stated base or create-event rule, and `advertisement_nonce` has no receiver-side acceptance window despite the replay control at 692 and the test at 868.
all_findings.why_it_matters: These are the exact values the deterministic reducer at lines 358-362 validates. Anything undefined here becomes a per-replica guess, and a per-replica guess in a state machine is a divergence bug. §12.2 requires golden fixtures for canonical events (815) and "unknown optional/required behavior" (817) — unspecifiable today.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a compact field table (extend §4.1 or add §5.4) covering the example-only fields with type, required/optional, and bound. Prioritize the values reducers branch on: enumerate the V1 `kind` namespace and the `actor_type`/`capture_level` enums, state whether `expected_entity_version` starts at 0 or 1 and whether create-kind events carry it, and give the discovery nonce cache size and acceptance window.
all_findings.verifier_note: The occurrence counts check out — all ten named identifiers appear exactly once, inside the examples, and `capture_level` appears at 326/525/973 with no enum. But the alarm is inflated and several sub-claims are uncharitable or self-refuting. RFC3339 for `expires_at` versus RFC3339Nano for event times is a plausible deliberate precision choice, not a disagreement. The `hlc` encoding barely matters because line 344 makes wall time and HLC display-only and non-authoritative — the finding quotes that line itself. The 'per-replica guess is a divergence bug' escalation does not hold: replicas run one implementation, and lines 292-294, 358-362, and 848 already pin versioning, deterministic recheck, and cross-version replication tests. The residual is a genuine reference-completeness gap concentrated in the fields a reducer actually branches on: the V1 `kind` namespace, `actor_type`/`capture_level` enums, `expected_entity_version` base and applicability, and the discovery nonce acceptance window behind the replay control at 692/868.

all_findings.title: Line 8's normative apparatus is decorative: 33 keyword uses across ~840 lines, no RFC 2119 citation, and hundreds of bare-prose requirements
all_findings.problem: Line 8 declares `MUST`, `SHOULD`, and `MAY` normative but the document also uses `MUST NOT` (five times), and no RFC 2119/8174 citation is given.
all_findings.why_it_matters: With 4% of the requirement surface keyworded, an implementer or reviewer cannot distinguish a hard requirement from prose narration, and a release gate that says "no fail-open flag" (770) has no defined bindingness. It also makes the doc unciteable in review: "is line 552 a MUST?" has no answer.
all_findings.recommendation: One-line fix at line 8: cite RFC 2119 and RFC 8174, add `MUST NOT` to the declared set, and state that unmarked declarative statements are requirements unless marked `MAY` or 'optional'. Do not retro-fit keywords across §2.1, §8.4, §10, and §11.
all_findings.verifier_note: The counts are accurate (MUST 23 including 5 MUST NOT, SHOULD 2, MAY 8) and line 8 does omit MUST NOT while citing no RFC — a real, tiny inconsistency. Everything built on top of that is style preference dressed as a defect. Line 8 states which words are normative when they appear in caps; it does not claim to be the document's only source of requirements, and headings like 'Required controls:' (690), 'Required behavior' (657), and 'Required unit/component subjects' (802) are unambiguous in English. 'Decorative', '4% of the requirement surface', and 'unciteable in review' are rhetoric: a reviewer asking 'is line 552 a MUST?' can read line 552, which is an imperative in a section titled by an invariant at line 92. Retro-fitting keywords onto every bullet in §2.1, §8.4, §10, and the failure table would add hundreds of words of ceremony to a document whose whole style is compression, and the finding's own alternative (b) concedes the current prose already reads as requirements.

all_findings.title: Front and back matter: no author/owner/reviewers/changelog/approval, no glossary, 4 references for ~15 load-bearing dependencies, and ADR gaps
all_findings.problem: §18 lists four references and omits the dependencies the design cannot be built without. §8 delegates watcher, indexing, block transfer, resume, conflict-copy, and versioning behavior to Syncthing and constrains ~15 of its settings by name, with no Syncthing reference or minimum version; §7 assumes the MCP specification throughout and commits to a Claude Code adapter (486, ADR-012) while citing only Codex product docs; §6.1/§11 mandate 'the Raft library's production stable store' (419, 726, ADR-020) without identifying a candidate.
all_findings.why_it_matters: For a greenfield doc whose stated bar is "no other context needed", an unattributed draft with no reviewers cannot be approved, and an implementer cannot resolve any of the semantic questions in F1/F5 because the upstream specs are not even identified. The Syncthing omission is the sharpest: §8 delegates watcher, indexing, transfer, resume, and conflict logic to it and then constrains ~15 of its config settings by name.
all_findings.recommendation: Add references for Syncthing (docs plus minimum pinned version), the MCP specification revision, Claude Code's MCP configuration docs, and the candidate embedded Raft library and stable store. Author/reviewer/changelog metadata and the Go-over-Rust and at-rest-encryption ADRs are worth adding but are template and backlog items, not document defects.
all_findings.verifier_note: Verified: lines 1-6 carry only Status/Date/Revision/Audience; there is no glossary; §18 has exactly four references, none for Syncthing, the MCP specification, the Raft library, or any RFC; and neither the Go-over-Rust decision (719-730) nor the no-at-rest-encryption posture (713-715) has an ADR. But the finding bundles a genuine gap with house-style preferences and with a category error. §17 is titled 'ADR Backlog' — a backlog is by definition incomplete, so an absent ADR is a queued item, not a documented inconsistency. Author/reviewer/changelog/approval-workflow metadata is a template convention of the reviewing organization, not something this document contradicts, and 'an unattributed draft cannot be approved' is an assertion about a process not described here. The glossary point duplicates F9. What genuinely survives is §18: §8 delegates watcher, indexing, transfer, resume, conflict, and versioning semantics to Syncthing and then constrains roughly fifteen of its settings by name (536, 552-554, 601), and §7 assumes MCP throughout while citing only Codex's product docs even though ADR-012 and line 486 commit to a Claude adapter.

all_findings.title: Terminology drift: eight terms carry multiple meanings or multiple names for one thing
all_findings.problem: Several load-bearing terms carry multiple meanings or multiple names. 'trust epoch' (143, a recovery generation) collides with the 30-minute `credential_epoch` (197, 238, 251) inside the security sections, where a misreading means renewing the wrong thing. 'strict writes' (139) is a one-off for 'strong'. 'eligible' is used with three different unstated predicates (26/571 peer selection, 51/580 files, 834 replicas), and 'eligible up-to-date source' at 571 hides an actual selection rule. The protected/control-file set has five names plus an event kind and a CLI verb (96, 578, 617, 644, 673, §8.4 heading, 872). 'Session' means the collaboration (152), the device set (60), a TLS connection (253), and an agent instance.
all_findings.why_it_matters: In a document this terse, a term used twice with two meanings is the whole definition. "Eligible up-to-date source" (571) is an actual implementation decision hiding behind an adjective, and the trust-epoch/credential-epoch collision is in the security section where a misreading means renewing the wrong thing.
all_findings.recommendation: Rename 'trust epoch' at 143 to 'recovery generation' so 'epoch' means credentials only; replace 'strict' with 'strong' at 139; state the predicate at each 'eligible' site, at minimum for 571 (owner/editor role, applied index equal to committed index, no unresolved conflicts); pick one name for the protected-file set and use it at all seven sites including the event kind and CLI verb; and use 'connection' rather than 'sessions' at 253. A short glossary or three added §4.1 rows covering strong, collaboration/session/agent session, and member/peer/device would cover the rest.
all_findings.verifier_note: Every claim is grep-verifiable and the collisions are real in a document whose terseness makes a term's second use its definition. 'trust epoch' (143) versus `credential_epoch`/'30-minute epoch' (197, 238, 251) are two unrelated counters sharing a word, both in the security sections. 'strict writes' at 139 is the document's only use of 'strict' in that sense against 'strong' at 20, 30, 33, 50, 60-61, 88, 664-665, 942. 'eligible' at 26, 51, 571, 580, and 834 carries at least three predicates and is defined for none — 'eligible up-to-date peer' at 26/571 is a real source-selection rule hiding in an adjective. The protected-file set is named differently at 96, 578, 617, 644, 673, the §8.4 heading, and 872. 'session' spans the collaboration (152), the device set (60), a TLS connection (253), and an agent instance. Two sub-claims are softer than stated and I have dropped them: 'connector' at 539 is defined functionally by the surrounding two sentences, and 'strong' is defined operationally by lines 20, 88, and 128 even though the word itself is never glossed. The residual set still warrants the fix.

all_findings.title: The 28-pair arithmetic is correct, but per-pair tunnel/connector fan-out is unstated and the 32-agent cap is not scoped to device or session
all_findings.problem: The scope of the 32-agent figure is ambiguous. Line 45 and the benchmark axis at 890 ('8 devices/32 agents') read as session-wide, while the same-device regression at 861-864 requires '32-session responsiveness' on one device — an 8x difference in per-daemon load for a number that is both a capacity commitment and a benchmark axis. The document also does not say whether 32 is an enforced cap or a tested target. Separately, whether an authorized pair carries one tunnel or one per direction (538-540) is unstated, though line 542 already requires the relevant bounds.
all_findings.why_it_matters: "32 agents" is a §14-adjacent capacity commitment and a benchmark axis, so it must be a single number with a single scope; a daemon sized for 4 local MCP processes behaves differently from one sized for 32. The tunnel fan-out feeds directly into the per-device connection, memory, and file-descriptor budgets the doc asks to be bounded.
all_findings.recommendation: State whether 32 concurrent agent instances is per device or session-wide and whether it is enforced or merely a tested target, then align line 45, line 864, and line 890 to that choice. Optionally add one clause to 538-540 saying whether a pair carries one tunnel or one per direction; the numeric caps alluded to at 542 can stay as bounds without figures.
all_findings.verifier_note: Credit where due: the finding verifies the 28-pair arithmetic and confirms both sites are worded compatibly, so there is no error there. Of the two residual gaps, one is minor by the document's own conventions and one is real. The tunnel fan-out question is a bounded-limit-without-a-number: line 542 already mandates bounding 'stream count, byte rate, backpressure, idle/lifetime limits', line 968 restates it as a risk, and whether the concurrent-tunnel bound works out to 28 or 56 does not change any decision in the document. The 32-agent scope ambiguity is the real one: line 45's 'coordinate 2-8 devices and up to 32 concurrent agent instances' reads most naturally as session-wide and line 890 benchmarks '8 devices/32 agents', while line 864 requires '32-session responsiveness' on a single device in the same-device regression — an 8x difference in per-daemon sizing.

all_findings.title: Per-entry leader signature over (term, log_index, previous_entry_hash) is not implementable on Raft and creates two validly-signed entries at one index
all_findings.problem: Lines 301-304 and step 3 (356) require the leader to assign term/log_index/previous_entry_hash and sign them BEFORE proposing to Raft. Two unresolved problems.
