(1) Feasibility: mainstream embedded Raft libraries selected at line 727 do not expose the assigned index to the proposer pre-commit - hashicorp/raft Apply/ApplyLog and etcd/raft Propose both seal the payload and assign term/index internally, with no index-reservation API. The only workaround is serializing every proposal against LastIndex()+1, which races leader no-op and configuration entries and forbids the pipelining the line 889 benchmarks assume. (2) The hash chain's domain is undefined and self-contradictory: previous_entry_hash sits in the leader-signed consensus block (336), but line 367 says rejected commands and Raft config entries consume indices so accepted-event indices may have gaps. If the chain covers all Raft entries, a nonvoter receiving only accepted events in bounded signed batches (371) can never recompute it; if it covers accepted events only, the leader cannot compute it at propose time because acceptance is decided by the deterministic apply in step 5. Secondarily, chain continuity is absent from the step 5 recheck list (358-360) even though line 373 makes a snapshot chain digest load-bearing for joiners.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the central integrity mechanism of the coordination plane and invariant "No split-brain strong state" (line 88) leans on it. As written an implementer must invent the chain domain, will discover mid-implementation that the chosen Raft library cannot supply pre-commit indices, and will either fork the library, serialize all proposals, or quietly drop the leader signature - a large architectural rework. Meanwhile a divergent, validly-signed phantom entry at a reused index is exactly the artifact an audit or snapshot verifier would accept.
all_findings.recommendation: Decouple the hash chain from Raft ordering: drop leader-assigned term/log_index/previous_entry_hash from the signed proposal, let Raft own ordering, and have every replica derive the chain deterministically at apply over ACCEPTED events only (chain_n = H(domain_sep || chain_n-1 || canonical_accepted_event_n), stated hash and chain_version), recording observed (term, log_index) as unsigned local provenance. If a leader attestation is wanted, make it a separate periodic committed checkpoint signed over (term, applied_index, chain_digest) proposed AFTER apply, which is expressible on standard library APIs. Add chain continuity to the step 5 recheck list and name the trust anchor for snapshot chain digests plus who verifies them. Do not restate that uncommitted entries are not events - lines 88 and 305 already cover that.
all_findings.verifier_note: Sub-claim (a) is refuted by the doc's own text: line 88 ("Only quorum-committed Raft entries are accepted") and lines 303-305 ("Raft commitment and deterministic state-machine validation, not either signature alone, produce an accepted event") already state that a leader-signed but uncommitted entry is not an event, so the 'two validly-signed entries at one index' artifact never becomes history, and snapshots (373) are built from committed state. Line 696 repeats the same pairing. Sub-claim (d) is real but trivial (chain continuity is absent from the 358-360 recheck list). Sub-claims (b) and (c) survive and are the real defect. (b) is a genuine internal contradiction the doc never resolves: line 336 puts previous_entry_hash in the leader-signed consensus block, while line 367 says rejected commands and Raft config entries consume indices so 'accepted event indices may have gaps' - the chain's domain (all Raft entries vs. accepted events only) is never stated, and if it is accepted-events-only the leader provably cannot compute it at propose time because acceptance is decided at apply (358-362). (c) is substantively correct on the library question: hashicorp/raft's Apply/ApplyLog and etcd/raft's Propose both take a sealed payload and assign term/index internally, with no reservation API; the only way to pre-sign an index is to serialize proposals and gamble on LastIndex()+1 against leader no-op and configuration entries, which is brittle and kills pipelining. That is a feasibility problem line 966 does not confront. Not a blocker because the safety story does not actually depend on the pre-commit signature (88/305 make commitment authoritative), so the fix is a localized redesign of one signed block, not a security hole.

all_findings.title: "Equal projection digests" is undefined and contradicts cross-version replication; no rule freezes reducer semantics per schema version
all_findings.problem: Line 834-836 makes 'equal projection digests' a harness pass/fail criterion, but 'projection digest' appears nowhere else in the document: the covered tables, row ordering, per-row canonical encoding, hash function, digest versioning, and the meaning of 'eligible' are all unspecified, so implementers will guess (SQLite page hashes are nondeterministic across vacuum/free-list/rowid reuse; unordered SELECT is not stable). Separately, the doc never states the invariant that makes deterministic replication safe across releases: that the reducer outcome for a given (event kind, schema_version) is frozen. Without it, a v1.1 daemon that 'fixes' a transition rule (e.g. blocked -> done, line 431) accepts an event at index N that a v1.0 replica stored as a structured rejection (362), diverging both replicas permanently while both believe they are deterministic. Line 782's compatibility-coverage gate and 819's migration+replay digest fixture point at the concern but state no invariant, and cross-version replication is an explicit scenario (848).
all_findings.why_it_matters: Divergent state machines in a system whose whole premise is "deterministic reducers" (line 24) and "one winner for strong claims" (line 50) means two devices disagree about who owns a task while both believe they are committed and correct. There is no production-time divergence detector. This must be settled before any reducer is written, because it constrains how every future behavior change ships.
all_findings.recommendation: Define the digest normatively in section 12.3: an ordered fold over a named set of projection tables, rows canonically encoded with explicit field order and sorted by primary key, with a digest_version and a stated hash. Define 'eligible' (recommend: same digest_version and same schema_version) so scenario 8's cross-version replicas are excluded from the exact-equality assertion, and if a cross-version core subset must match, declare it. Add to section 6.2 a normative invariant that reducer behavior for an existing (kind, schema_version) MUST NOT change and that changed semantics require a new kind or new schema_version gated on committed capability, and add it to line 783's non-mergeable list. Drop the claim that scenario 8 and line 834 are unsatisfiable.
all_findings.verifier_note: The undefined-term claim checks out: 'projection digest' appears exactly once in the file (line 835), with no covered tables, row order, row encoding, hash, or definition of 'eligible'. The frozen-reducer invariant is also genuinely absent. But two of the three escalating claims are overstated. First, scenario 8 (848) and the line 834 assertion are not 'mutually unsatisfiable': line 834 is scoped to 'eligible replicas', which is exactly the hedge that excludes differing-version replicas - the defect is that 'eligible' is undefined, not that the two requirements contradict. Second, 'no detection, silent and permanent' ignores line 782, which forbids merging reducer, migration, protocol, consensus, or security changes 'without compatibility coverage', and 819's 'migration+replay digest' and 848's cross-version replication scenario, which are the doc's (partial, test-time) answer. The residual defect - define the digest normatively and state that reducer outcome for a given (kind, schema_version) is frozen - is real and cheap, but it is a specification gap, not a design that cannot work.

all_findings.title: Quorum loss silently kills ALL peer connectivity within 30 minutes, contradicting two stated guarantees, and the recovery path for credential-expired survivors is undefined
all_findings.problem: Recovery from permanent majority loss is underspecified in a way that leaves one case with no path at all. Lines 142-144 require 'explicit owner-approved recovery into a new trust epoch from the last verified committed state' and line 646 exposes recover-quorum, but the doc never states whether recovery is performed offline on a single device (it must be, since by then all credentials have expired per 665/667 and no peer can connect), how non-owner survivors are re-admitted and learn the new epoch when they cannot open any authenticated channel, how the new epoch's genesis links to the original immutable genesis record (168-170 defines no successor), or who may initiate recovery when the OWNER device is one of the lost ones - line 181 makes invite/role/voter changes owner-only, so an editor-only survivor set appears permanently unrecoverable. Scenario 17 (858) stops at 'fail closed' and never exercises the post-credential-expiry state.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the last-resort availability path for a system explicitly targeting flaky LAN/VPN environments (2.2) and 2-device sessions (line 60). As written, an ordinary event - one of three laptops closes its lid and one loses Wi-Fi - degrades in 30 minutes from "strong writes queue" to "total session outage including file sync", and the doc's own guarantees say otherwise. An implementer cannot build `recover-quorum` without inventing the re-admission and owner-absent policy, and each guess produces a different security posture.
all_findings.recommendation: Specify recover-quorum end to end: offline single-device operation, how survivors are re-admitted (re-pair with two-sided confirmation vs. an epoch-bump proof), how the successor epoch links to the genesis record, and an explicit owner-absent policy (e.g. an offline-verifiable owner recovery key per line 708, or a committed break-glass authorization). Extend scenario 17 to lose quorum, let all credentials expire, then recover. Do NOT change lines 550 or 941 - they describe leader loss, which the doc correctly separates from quorum loss at rows 663/665; the availability coupling itself is already stated at 35, 448, 665, 667, 97 and risk 965, so at most add a one-line pointer to the 665 row.
all_findings.verifier_note: The headline contradiction claim is wrong. Lines 550 and 941 are both about LEADER loss, which the doc deliberately distinguishes from quorum loss in adjacent failure rows (663 'Leader loss | Elect; direct reads/sync continue' vs 665 'Quorum loss | Queue strong work; stop credential renewal'). With quorum intact the leader is replaced and credentials keep renewing, so both statements are true as written and nothing is falsified. The coupling the reviewer says is hidden is stated repeatedly and precisely: line 35, line 448 ('only while credentials remain valid'), line 665, line 667 ('Expired credential | Close sessions; renewal-only re-auth after quorum'), invariant 97, line 254-255, and risk 2 at line 965. The consequence is a deliberate derivation from 'no insecure minority renewal', not an unnoticed cliff; making it more prominent is editorial. What genuinely survives is narrow: the recovery path at 142-144 / 646 / 676 / 858 never says whether recover-quorum can run with zero peer connectivity, how survivors are re-admitted, how the new epoch links to the genesis record (168-170 has no successor concept), or what happens when the owner device is among the lost, given that 181 makes voter/role changes owner-only. Compaction-style phase deferral (927 'voter/quorum recovery') partly excuses the detail level.

all_findings.title: Credential expiry - the sole bound on stale-partition access - is enforced against unsynchronized local wall clocks with no skew allowance
all_findings.problem: Credential expiry is the doc's stated bound on stale-partition access (254-255) and a required control (694-695), but it is validated at 246-248 against each peer's local wall clock with no specified maximum skew, clock source, or monotonic anchoring - 'skew' appears in the document only at line 445 (leases) and line 830 (harness fault), never for credentials, and section 2.2 permits networks without Internet or DHCP so NTP may be absent. A peer whose clock is slow by more than the line 252 overlap keeps accepting a revoked-then-partitioned device's epoch credential past its committed expiry, silently exceeding the documented bound on peers that have not observed the revocation (253). The five-minute early renewal and two-minute overlap at 251-252 absorb small drift but are not stated as a skew policy and set no ceiling.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Line 254-255 is the doc's answer to "what stops a stale or ex-member from acting", and section 10 line 694-695 lists "bounded stale partition lifetime" as a required control. That bound is only as good as the clocks, and the doc neither bounds them nor bounds the damage. Skew is also a first-class harness fault (line 830 "skew/rollover"), so the tests will hit undefined behavior.
all_findings.recommendation: State the time model for credential validation: a maximum tolerated skew applied asymmetrically (never lenient past expiry; lenient at issue time so a fast clock cannot self-isolate), monotonic-clock anchoring for the connection lifetime cap at line 251, and a requirement to surface gross skew as a health signal per 756 (e.g. comparing committed sequenced_at against local time). Note explicitly that revocation is the primary control and expiry the backstop for peers that have not observed it, and give the resulting worst-case stale-access window as epoch + skew.
all_findings.verifier_note: The absence is real: grep confirms 'skew' appears only at 445 (leases) and 830 (harness fault), so credential validation at 246-248 has no stated skew allowance, clock source, or monotonicity requirement, and 2.2 does allow networks with no Internet/NTP. But the reviewer credits none of the existing slack. Line 251-252 already requires renewing about five minutes early, permits up to two minutes of epoch overlap, and caps connection lifetime - which absorbs ordinary drift and directly blunts the 'fast clock self-isolates' scenario for anything under ~5 minutes. Line 253 makes committed revocation the immediate control and 254-255 frames expiry as the bound only for isolated partitions. So the damage is a widened worst case on an already-explicitly-approximate backstop, not a broken control; and line 830 does schedule skew as a test fault. This is a missing normative number with security relevance, which per severity discipline is minor rather than major.

all_findings.title: Lease expiry has no time source when there is no leader, the skew allowance has no number, and two independent expiry paths are unreconciled
all_findings.problem: Two lease-timing details are unspecified. (1) 'the bounded clock-skew allowance' at line 445 has no value anywhere in the document, and the leader's local clock is a trusted input to lease expiry with no requirement that it be monotonic-anchored or sanity-checked against discontinuous jumps. (2) Precedence is undefined between the two expiry paths: the committed lease deadline enforced by the leader (443-445) and the agent-disconnect grace expiry that 'releases leases' from the agent's host daemon (495-496). If an agent resumes with its capability inside grace after the leader has already expired the lease, the doc does not say which outcome is authoritative or that the resumed agent must recheck ownership. Related: because only the leader proposes expire commands, no lease can expire while the cluster is leaderless or without quorum (664-665); this follows from stated rules but its user-visible effect is never described. Impact is bounded by line 442, which makes leases advisory and bypassable by design.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Leases are the only concurrency control in shared-root mode and the only overlap signal in worktree mode; the shared-root risk is already acknowledged at line 977. An implementer must invent the skew number and the leaderless-expiry policy, and the resume-vs-expire race is exactly the kind of bug the line 844 harness scenario ("adapter resume/expiry/ID non-reuse") will surface as nondeterministic.
all_findings.recommendation: Give the skew allowance a number and a home (recommend committing it in the genesis policy at line 168 so all members agree), require the leader's expiry decision to use a monotonic-anchored clock and skip expiry after a discontinuous jump, and state precedence explicitly: the committed log is authoritative, resume never revives an expired lease, and a resumed agent MUST recheck lease ownership at its applied index. Add one sentence that leases cannot expire without a leader or quorum and what the UI shows, and add a 'leaderless across a lease deadline' harness fault. Drop the framing that leases are hard concurrency control - line 442 already says they are advisory.
all_findings.verifier_note: Sub-claim (b) is verified - the clock-skew allowance genuinely has no number anywhere (only occurrences are 445 and 830) and the leader's clock is an untyped trusted input to expiry. Sub-claim (a) is largely the documented behavior rather than a defect: leases are committed strong state, and line 665 already says quorum loss queues strong work while 664 queues proposals during elections, so 'no lease can expire without a leader' is the consistent consequence of stated rules, not an omission. Its blast radius is also much smaller than claimed because line 442 explicitly makes leases advisory ('Leases warn and reduce overlap; they cannot stop a same-user process from editing a path'), repeated at 513-514 and risk 977 - so a stalled expiry does not create a false mutual-exclusion guarantee, it withholds an advisory one. Sub-claim (c) is partly pre-answered: lease state is committed and reducers never consult local clocks (443), so a grace-period release is also a proposed command, and line 487 already requires version recheck; scenario 844 covers adapter resume/expiry. The residual is that precedence between the two paths is not spelled out and no scenario is leaderless across a deadline.

all_findings.title: Voter membership policy is unspecified: who becomes a voter as devices join, whether 2/4-voter configs exist, and the target count after removing a lost voter
all_findings.problem: Voter policy has two unstated pieces. (1) Admission (steps 7-8, 225-228) never states the default consensus role for a newly admitted device, and nothing in the TUI requirements (630-633) requires a persistent warning while voters < 3, so a session that legitimately starts with one voter (135) can grow to eight devices and silently retain zero fault tolerance despite line 136 scoping one voter to 'development or minimal sessions'. (2) 'up-to-date' is load-bearing at lines 26, 372, and 571 (bootstrap source and snapshot-serving eligibility, and implicitly promotion eligibility) but is never defined. Minor residual: line 857 / 675 read as remove-then-replace, but the resting configuration when no replacement device exists is unstated.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Voter set composition determines every availability property the doc promises (lines 32-33, 940) and gates the DS-03 outage. An implementer will guess - most likely "nonvoter by default, manual promotion" - and ship a product where the common 3-device session silently has one voter and no fault tolerance despite the doc recommending three. Scenario 16 cannot be written without answering (c).
all_findings.recommendation: Add two or three sentences to section 3: default consensus role on admission (recommend nonvoter), an explicit trigger for reaching three voters plus a persistent degraded-tolerance indicator in the TUI while voters < 3, a definition of 'up-to-date' (applied index within N of the committed index) used for promotion, snapshot service, and bootstrap eligibility, and the resting configuration allowed after a permanent voter removal with no replacement. Do not claim 2-voter configurations are ambiguous or that scenario 16 is unwritable - lines 20, 133, 139-140, 675 and 857 already constrain both.
all_findings.verifier_note: Two of the four sub-claims are answered by the text. (b) is effectively settled: line 20 states 1/3/5 voters, line 133 says odd counts are preferred, and lines 139-140 say plainly that 'No two-device configuration can preserve strict writes after either device fails; a third independent voting device is required' - so 2 voters is clearly not a resting configuration, and line 61 already distinguishes two-device sessions from three-voter failover. (c) has a scenario and a failure row: line 675 'Permanent voter loss with quorum | Safe remove/replace' and scenario 16 (857) 'Remove a permanently lost voter, add replacement, retain existing trust' read as remove-then-replace, with joint consensus (132) covering the transient even count; what is missing is only the resting-state rule if no replacement exists. (a) and (d) survive as genuine one-line policy gaps: the admission flow (225-227, step 8 at 226-228) never states the default consensus role, nothing requires a degraded-tolerance warning in the 630-633 TUI views, and 'up-to-date' (used at 26, 372, 571 for snapshot service and bootstrap eligibility) is never defined. These are cheap specification additions, not a design that cannot work.

all_findings.title: Compaction is one clause: no retention floor, no cursor-too-old behavior, no coordination with Raft snapshots, and no chain anchor for post-compaction history
all_findings.problem: Compaction is named only twice (59, 927) and never specified, and two consequences reach V1 mechanisms. (1) idempotency_keys (404) has no stated retention or GC rule; if it is pruned, retried mutations whose kinds are covered by neither the (device_id, agent_session_id, origin_sequence) constraint (414) nor expected_entity_version (324) - notably memory.append (435), activity.append, and POST /v1/acks (285) - can double-apply. (2) When compaction is designed, the doc will need a retained event floor, a defined 'cursor too old' response for GET /v1/events?after=N (281) so a client falls back to snapshot-plus-tail (372-374) instead of leaving a permanent hole in its events table (which would break the 834 digest equality), a rule tying the logical floor to the Raft snapshot index, and a designated trust anchor for pre-floor history now that the chain digest (373) is signed by a single 'up-to-date voter' rather than quorum. Note line 59's V1 target is session-lifetime history, so no cursor should fall below a floor in V1, and line 420 already pairs backup with a verified Raft snapshot/applied index.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Long-offline rejoin (line 53 "resume idempotently") and 1M-event catch-up (line 889) are both promised. Silent event holes are precisely the failure the line 836 harness assertion is meant to catch, and it will catch it only if a test happens to compact - no scenario in 12.3 does. Compaction also interacts with every verification story in the doc, so leaving it to phase 6 (line 927) invites a retrofit through the persistence and replication layers.
all_findings.recommendation: For V1, state an explicit retention for idempotency_keys that provably exceeds the maximum client retry window, and name which event kinds rely on the origin-sequence uniqueness constraint instead. For phase 6 (927), require compaction to advance the retained floor only via a committed command carrying the new floor and snapshot digest, require floor <= Raft snapshot index, add a cursor_too_old structured problem (293) with mandatory snapshot fallback, designate the trust anchor for pre-floor history and its countersignature policy, and add compaction-then-rejoin and compaction-then-snapshot-verify harness scenarios. Drop the claim that a week-long absence already overruns the floor - line 59 keeps session-lifetime history in V1.
all_findings.verifier_note: The grep confirms compaction appears only at lines 59 and 927, so it is genuinely unspecified - but line 59 is also the refutation of the central scenario: V1 targets 'session-lifetime coordination history with export before compaction', i.e. history is retained for the whole session, so the 'nonvoter offline for a week returns below the retained floor' case does not arise in V1, and line 927 places compaction in phase 6 hardening where its retention rules would be designed. Sub-claim (b) is partly covered by line 420, which already requires backup/export to pair a SQLite backup with 'a matching verified Raft snapshot/applied index'. Sub-claim (a)'s missing 'cursor_too_old' error is a concrete gap but sits inside an existing mechanism (293 structured problem responses, 372-374 snapshot-then-tail fallback), so it is an added problem type rather than new machinery. Sub-claim (c) about the chain losing its root is real but contingent on compaction existing, and (d) is real: idempotency_keys (404) has no stated retention, and the reviewer correctly notes that 414's uniqueness constraint and 324's expected_entity_version cover only some kinds while memory.append, activity.append, and POST /v1/acks are neither. Overall a phase-6 specification gap with one V1-relevant loose end.

all_findings.title: `hlc` and `created_at` are inside the signed body but declared display-only with no validation rule, and no HLC update rule exists
all_findings.problem: The `hlc` field (321) sits inside the origin-signed canonical event body and will therefore appear in every golden fixture (814) and signature test, yet it has no defined encoding, no receive-side advance rule, and no consumer anywhere in the document - five implementers will produce five incompatible encodings of a signed field. `created_at` (320) is likewise signed but excluded from the deterministic recheck list (358-360), so it is an unvalidated origin claim that is nonetheless durable and rendered. Line 344 already states that log_index defines order and wall time/HLC are display-only, which limits the harm, but no rule tells the TUI (630) or generated context (393) that they MUST NOT order history by created_at, and no deterministic bound is possible via the leader alone since prevalidation is non-authoritative (369).
all_findings.why_it_matters: Cheap to fix, but signed-and-unvalidated fields are how forged-event tests (line 873 "forged/replayed/oversized events") turn into ambiguity, and misleading provenance directly undermines section 7.3's premise that provenance display is a real control. Leaving `hlc` undefined also means five implementers produce five encodings that all appear in golden fixtures (line 814).
all_findings.recommendation: Preferred: drop `hlc` from V1 and say log_index is the only ordering, keeping created_at as an explicitly unvalidated origin claim that the UI MUST label as such and MUST NOT sort by. If it is kept, define its encoding and receive-side advance rule and add a deterministic apply-time bound expressed only in committed values (e.g. reject created_at outside a committed drift window around the entry's sequenced_at), add that check to the step 5 recheck list, and add a negative fixture. Do not argue that provenance display is already corrupted - line 344 makes log_index authoritative.
all_findings.verifier_note: The factual core holds: created_at and hlc are inside the origin-signed body (320-321, 342), are absent from the step 5 deterministic recheck list (358-360), and hlc has no defined encoding, no receive-side advance rule (the defining property of an HLC), and no named consumer anywhere in the document. The reviewer is also right that a leader-side bound would be non-deterministic and non-authoritative per 369. The harm narrative is overstated, though: line 344 already declares 'log_index defines order; wall time/HLC aid display and diagnosis only', so a UI or context.{json,md} that orders history by created_at is violating the doc rather than following it, and 715 already says signatures prove provenance, not content safety. Severity as filed (minor) is correct; the actionable residual is the undefined field in a canonically encoded, signed, golden-fixtured structure (814).

all_findings.title: Leader pre-rejection is unreplicated and not recorded, so the same retry can yield different outcomes across leaders
all_findings.problem: Line 369 already establishes that leader pre-rejection is not the authoritative state transition, but the client-facing contract is not stated: nothing says the pre-rejection response MUST be a distinctly typed retryable structured problem (293) that a client MUST retry against the current leader rather than treat as terminal, nor that it emits no durable audit event (128) and consumes no idempotency key. A client that treats a pre-rejection as final may abandon a claim a later leader would accept, and an operator may see a rejection in the UI with no committed trace - presenting as an unreproducible 'CLI said rejected but the task is claimed' report during the leader-churn scenarios at 851 and 855-856.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Small blast radius, but it makes the client contract nondeterministic in exactly the leader-churn scenarios the harness stresses (scenarios 11 and 15, lines 851 and 855-856), and it will present as an unreproducible "the CLI said rejected but the task is claimed" bug.
all_findings.recommendation: Add one sentence after line 369: pre-rejection MUST use a distinct retryable problem type, MUST NOT consume or record an idempotency key or emit a durable audit event, and clients MUST retry it against the current leader; optionally restrict it to conditions monotone in applied index. Do not assert the doc treats pre-rejection as authoritative - line 369 says the opposite.
all_findings.verifier_note: The doc already states the substance of the recommendation. Line 369 says a leader 'MAY pre-reject an obviously stale command but MUST NOT treat prevalidation as the authoritative state transition' - that is precisely 'pre-rejection is non-authoritative'. It also follows from step 7 (363-364), where the idempotency result is committed inside the SQLite transaction, that an uncommitted pre-rejection consumes no idempotency key; the reviewer's own interleaving is therefore the documented behavior of a non-authoritative optimization rather than a contradiction with line 362 (which governs committed invalid commands). What is genuinely missing is only the client-side half of the contract: the doc does not say the pre-rejection response must be a distinctly typed retryable problem (293) that clients MUST NOT treat as terminal, nor that it emits no durable audit event. That is a one-line clarification, below minor.

all_findings.title: Mixed-version daemons in one Raft cluster contradict the deterministic-reducer requirement; no skew policy exists
all_findings.problem: Lines 358-362 require every replica to deterministically apply and recheck each committed command, and line 834 makes equal projection digests at the same committed index a harness gate, but no section states normatively what a replica does when it encounters a committed entry it cannot deterministically apply (kind, field, or reducer branch it does not implement). Line 292-294's 'Unknown required capabilities fail closed' is scoped to wire messages in section 5.1 and does not cover an already-committed Raft entry. The doc's mixed-version protection is indirect: line 783 gates reducer/protocol changes on compatibility coverage, lines 816-820 require prior-protocol interop proofs, and lines 825/848 exercise current-plus-prior daemons in one cluster. Those make divergence a CI failure but never define the runtime rule or the supported skew window.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the one class of bug that silently destroys the correctness story the whole design rests on, and it will happen on the first real upgrade because nothing prevents a user from updating one laptop. It is unfixable after the fact: divergent projections are only detectable if you happen to compare digests, and the recovery path (line 143, new trust epoch from last verified committed state) is the heaviest one in the doc.
all_findings.recommendation: Add one normative subsection to section 5.3 stating: (a) a per-command minimum-apply-version or feature gate, with the rule that a replica which cannot deterministically apply a committed entry halts and refuses to advance its applied index rather than substituting a local rejection; (b) the supported version-skew window (e.g. N-1) and the requirement that new reducer semantics ship dark and activate only via a committed capability-enable entry; (c) a TUI/CLI blocker state for a halted replica. No new tests are needed for the mixed-version digest comparison itself - lines 825, 834, and 848 already cover it; add only the halt-safely assertion.
all_findings.verifier_note: The factual core survives: no line in the file states a supported version-skew policy or an apply-time gating/halt rule for committed Raft entries, and lines 358-362 do require every replica to deterministically recheck schema/sequence/transition. But the blocker framing and several sub-claims do not survive. (a) The doc does constrain the direction the reviewer says is absent: line 783 makes 'Protocol, migration, reducer, consensus, or security changes cannot merge without compatibility coverage' a merge gate, lines 816-820 require proving 'previous protocol interop, unknown optional/required behavior', and line 626 requires 'reviewed CodeComm releases with compatibility/rollback tests'. Under those rules a reducer change that made a prior version reject a command could not merge, so the doc forbids the scenario without naming the mechanism. (b) The recommendation to 'add a test that mixed-version projection digests are compared' is already covered: line 825 puts 'current/retained prior daemons' in the same harness cluster, line 848 is scenario 8 'Current/previous version and schema replication', and line 834's equal-projection-digest assertion applies to 'eligible replicas at the same committed index' in that mixed-version harness. (c) Line 292-294 'Unknown required capabilities fail closed' is indeed scoped to wire messages in section 5.1 and does not define apply-time behavior, so that part of the critique holds. What is genuinely missing is one normative paragraph: what a replica does when it cannot deterministically apply a committed entry (halt vs. reject), and how new reducer semantics are activated. That is a real specification gap worth fixing before phase 3, not a design that cannot work.

all_findings.title: Post-bootstrap Git history diverges permanently; worktree publication depends on an unresolved Open Question
all_findings.problem: Open Question 1 (lines 950-951) and the hedge at line 594 ('Ongoing commit/ref exchange, if included') leave unresolved a consequence the doc never spells out: because line 591-593 syncs working-tree content but not refs, indexes, or objects, a commit on device A leaves B's HEAD/index at the bootstrap commit while B's tree holds A's post-commit content, so git status on B reports the whole delta as uncommitted and a commit on B forks history. Section 8.3 does not describe this state, does not say who commits or rebases, and does not define whether a published proposal (line 509) is renderable when its base_commit is unresolvable locally.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The default agent isolation mode cannot be implemented without answering Open Question 1, and the answer changes section 8.2, 8.3, the role table, and delivery phases 4 and 5. An implementer will guess "working-tree-only" (the cheaper reading of line 594), ship it, and discover that the flagship feature — multiple agents on isolated worktrees publishing reviewed proposals — has no working verification path.
all_findings.recommendation: Keep Open Question 1 but add two or three sentences to 8.3 stating the working-tree-only consequence explicitly (receiver HEAD/index lag, git status shows synced content as local change, per line 77 CodeComm never merges), and state that a published proposal is verifiable from its per-path digests and patch metadata alone so base_commit is provenance rather than a resolution requirement. If the answer to OQ1 is 'include ref exchange', name the authenticated bare remote or incremental-bundle endpoint and add a git_base_missing state; if it is 'exclude', say so and record the divergent-history handling.
all_findings.verifier_note: The mechanism the reviewer describes is real and the doc leaves it open, but the 'cannot be implemented' claim rests on an invented dependency. Line 509 says the agent publishes the proposal 'into the canonical synchronized tree' with 'base commit, paths, digests, and patch/commit metadata' - the content itself travels as working-tree bytes via Syncthing, and the receiver can verify the published per-path digests against its synced tree and render the diff from the included patch metadata. Resolving base_commit as a git object is not required for either. So 'B can neither verify the digest chain nor render a diff' overstates the consequence. The residual observation is accurate and useful: with working-tree-only sync, a receiver's index/HEAD stay at the bootstrap commit while its tree carries the sender's post-commit content, so git status shows the whole delta as local, and the doc never says who commits, who rebases, or how divergent local histories are reconciled. That is exactly Open Question 1 (lines 950-951), explicitly hedged at line 594 ('if included'), and line 77 already declares no automatic merge a non-goal. Per the acknowledged-open-question rule this is not a blocker; implementation of the default worktree mode can proceed on the content-plus-patch-metadata reading.

all_findings.title: Long-lived device identity keys have no lifecycle: no rotation, no expiry, no re-enrollment, no backup, and revoked keys are not stated to be retained for history verification
all_findings.problem: Line 302-305 rests history verifiability on enrolled device identity keys, but the doc never states that revoked or superseded identity public keys are retained (presumably in `devices`, line 406) so past signatures remain verifiable after revocation - revocation is described only as closing sessions and removing the device (lines 668, 549). Separately, line 419-420 scopes backup to SQLite plus a matching Raft snapshot and never says whether excluding identity keys and credentials from backup is a deliberate choice with an accepted consequence. The re-pairing and voter-replacement mechanics for a lost or reinstalled device do exist (lines 141-142, 857, 905) but are not tied together as a named procedure.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Every trust decision in the system chains to this key, and the doc gives it less operational care than the keys it rotates every 30 minutes. Reinstalling an OS or replacing a laptop is a routine event for a 2-8 personal-device tool, and today it silently costs the user their authorship continuity and a voter slot with no documented procedure.
all_findings.recommendation: Add two normative sentences to 4.1: revoked and superseded identity public keys are retained indefinitely for historical signature verification, and revocation removes authorization but not verifiability. Add one sentence to 6.1 stating that identity private keys are deliberately not covered by backup/export and that a lost credential store means the device re-pairs as a new identity and its voter slot is replaced per lines 141-142. Identity-key rotation may stay out of V1 given the rationale at 302-305, but say so.
all_findings.verifier_note: The grep result holds - every rotation/expiry hit in the file (lines 23, 235-255, 984) is about the 30-minute transport credential, and there is no identity-key rotation, expiry, or re-enrollment text. But three of the four sub-claims are weaker than stated. (1) 'the doc never argues why' identity keys are long-lived is wrong: lines 302-305 give the reason explicitly - 'Both signatures use enrolled device identity keys, not rotating transport keys, so history remains verifiable.' Long-lived device identity with rotating transport credentials is the deliberate, stated architecture, not an oversight. (2) Key theft from the OS credential store (lines 164-165, 708-709) requires a compromised local OS account, which line 687-688 places outside the V1 boundary; so 'no compromise recovery' partly falls outside scope, leaving revocation (line 668) as the in-scope answer. (3) The lost/reinstalled-device path is largely composable from existing text: line 141-142 covers remove/replace of a permanently lost voter 'without re-pairing existing members', scenario 16 (line 857) tests it, section 4.4 covers re-pairing, and line 905 gates replace-voter at release. The genuinely uncovered items are narrower: the doc never states that revoked and superseded public keys are retained in `devices` for historical signature verification (needed to make the line 302-305 claim true over time), and line 419-420 never says whether excluding identity keys from backup is deliberate.

all_findings.title: 30-minute quorum-authorized TLS rotation: benefit is narrow, the availability cost is a hard offline cliff, and the doc never argues the tradeoff or the interval
all_findings.problem: The 30-minute credential epoch (lines 23, 238) is never justified numerically and is not stated to be a configurable committed policy value, even though it sets the hard ceiling on how long a minority partition keeps working (lines 33-35, 448, 665, 667). Nothing specifies what the user sees as expiry approaches: line 632 requires the 'expired' state be distinct, which is post-hoc, and there is no pre-expiry countdown or warning state. Note that lines 664, 550, and 941 concern leader loss with quorum intact, where renewal continues, so they are not in conflict with the cliff.
all_findings.why_it_matters: For a personal 2-8 device tool, a partition lasting more than 30 minutes is ordinary (a laptop on a hotel network, a device asleep, one of three voters at home). The design converts a partial outage into a total one, and an implementer reading lines 664/941 will build UX that promises continuity the credential layer will revoke.
all_findings.recommendation: Add one paragraph to 4.5 giving the rationale for the epoch length, making it a committed policy value with a stated default and range, and requiring that impending credential expiry surface as a distinct TUI/CLI state with a countdown well before the cliff (distinct from the post-expiry state at line 632). Add one sentence distinguishing leader-loss continuity (lines 664, 550, 941) from minority-partition expiry so the two are not conflated by implementers.
all_findings.verifier_note: The claimed contradiction - the strongest part of this finding - is a misread. Lines 664, 550, and 941 are all about *leader* loss, not quorum loss. With quorum intact, a lost leader is replaced by election (line 663, target line 937 p95 <5 s) and credential renewal resumes through any voter (line 242), so tunnels and transfers genuinely do continue and no 30-minute cliff applies. The cliff applies only to a *minority* partition, and the doc states that consequence plainly and repeatedly rather than hiding it: line 33-35 ('direct sync among reachable peers continue only until current credentials expire'), line 448 (same), line 665 ('Quorum loss: stop credential renewal'), line 667 ('Expired credential: close sessions'), invariant line 97 ('No insecure minority renewal'), risk 2 (line 965), and the benefit is argued at lines 253-255. So this is an explicitly owned tradeoff, not an unreconciled one, and target 941 does not need changing. What survives is narrow: the 30-minute value is never justified or made a committed policy parameter, and no pre-expiry warning is specified - line 632 requires only that the 'expired' state be distinct, i.e. after the fact.

all_findings.title: Discovery datagram's stated privacy properties are not delivered by its own schema
all_findings.problem: The datagram at lines 193-204 carries a plaintext `session_id` that is stable for the entire collaboration, plus monotonic `committed_membership_index` and `credential_epoch` values. Against the hostile-LAN threat model at line 684, a passive observer can group all of a user's devices into one collaboration and recognize that collaboration again on another network, and can infer session age and membership-change frequency from the counters. Line 207-208's enumerated claim is literally accurate - it never asserts unlinkability, and `advertising_key_digest` is correctly a rotating epoch value rather than an identity fingerprint - but readers will take it as broader than it is.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The doc makes a specific privacy claim that its own message format contradicts, so a reviewer or implementer will believe discovery is privacy-preserving and will not fix it. On a shared office or conference LAN — the exact environment section 2.2 targets — this is a persistent device-linkage beacon.
all_findings.recommendation: Replace the plaintext `session_id` with a per-epoch tag derived from the current epoch key (recognizable to members, uncorrelatable across epochs by strangers), and either drop or coarsen `committed_membership_index` and `credential_epoch`, both of which a peer can learn over mTLS after connecting. Restate lines 206-208 to say precisely what a passive same-link observer can learn rather than only what is absent. Gating `pairing_open` to windows when an invite is actually outstanding is a cheap addition on top of the line 232 rate limits.
all_findings.verifier_note: The privacy-claim-contradiction framing does not hold, but the underlying linkability observation does. Line 207-208 makes an enumerated claim - no workspace/device/user names, paths, stable identity fingerprints, secrets, tasks, or activity - and the schema at 193-204 honors every item on that list. In particular `advertising_key_digest` is the rotating epoch key digest, not an identity fingerprint (lines 197-198, 208-210), which shows the author specifically avoided the stable-fingerprint beacon the reviewer is worried about. So the doc does not assert unlinkability and its own claim is literally accurate; 'its own message format contradicts its claim' is overstated. Also, line 189 pins TTL/hop-limit to 1, confining the beacon to the local link, and line 232's rate limits are the stated invite-guessing mitigation. What survives is a legitimate residual: a plaintext `session_id` stable for the whole collaboration lets a passive observer on a hostile LAN (threat model line 684) group a user's devices and recognize them across networks, and the two monotonic counters leak change frequency and session age. Worth fixing, but this is passive same-link metadata, not a broken security control.

all_findings.title: Section 12 has no property-based, model-based, or deterministic-simulation testing, despite risk 3 naming Raft integration as a safety hazard
all_findings.problem: Section 12 addresses risk 3 (lines 966-967, incorrect Raft integration can violate safety) entirely with example-based techniques: enumerated scenarios (lines 840-859), a named fault list (829-832), golden fixtures (813-820), and seeded nightly soak/chaos (892-893). There is no property-based testing over reducers and canonical encoding, and no deterministic simulation mode - line 781's 'Random tests record seed/trace' records a seed but nothing guarantees a multi-node failure is replayable from it, since the harness uses real time and real scheduling. Cross-replica digest equality (834), snapshot/replay equivalence (805), real-Raft/real-SQLite rules (811-812), and boundary fault injection (829-832) already cover much of the ground, so this is a strengthening gap rather than an absent safety net.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Enumerated scenarios only find the interleavings someone imagined. The safety violations risk 3 warns about live in the interleavings nobody imagined, and a nightly chaos run that fails once every 200 runs without a deterministic replay is effectively unactionable. The rest of section 12 is unusually strong, which makes this the conspicuous gap.
all_findings.recommendation: Add to 12.2 a property-based suite over reducers and canonical encoding (encode/decode roundtrip, apply-order determinism, idempotent replay, CAS single-winner) with shrinking, and to 12.3 a deterministic mode built on the clock and failpoint seams already required at lines 794-797, so a harness failure is replayable from a seed rather than only recorded. State explicitly that a TLA+/Stateright model of the credential-epoch and membership state machine is out of V1 scope and that lines 811-812, 829-834 are what compensates.
all_findings.verifier_note: The factual claim checks out: grep finds no property-based, model-based, linearizability, TLA+, or deterministic-simulation testing anywhere; the only near hits are 'simulated Codex/Claude clients' (line 825) and 'MCP simulators' (line 885), and line 781 is indeed only a seed/trace hygiene rule. Risk 3 (lines 966-967) does name Raft integration as a safety hazard. But 'major' overstates it, because the doc already carries most of the assurance the reviewer wants from these techniques by other means: line 834 asserts cross-replica projection-digest equality after quiescence over a mixed-version cluster, line 805 requires snapshot-plus-replay equivalence and deterministic projection rebuild, lines 811-812 forbid mocking real SQLite and real three-voter Raft, lines 829-832 inject partitions/truncation/crashes exactly at the Raft and SQLite boundaries, lines 794-797 provide clock and failpoint seams, and lines 876-878 mandate continuous fuzzing of event/batch/snapshot decoding. Scenarios 3, 5, 6, 9, 15, 18 cover the specific safety properties. This is a 'would strengthen an already-strong section' recommendation about test technique, not a defect that blocks implementation or invalidates the strategy. Under a simplicity-tradeoffs lens it also has real cost.

all_findings.title: Concrete V1 scope cuts: several mechanisms carry full cost for a property the design already gets elsewhere
all_findings.problem: Section 13 lists six delivery phases but never states what is explicitly deferred past V1, so scope is implied rather than visible. Two specific items carry canonical-format cost for weak V1 value: `hlc` (line 328) is a signed canonical event field with golden-fixture and cross-platform-signature-stability obligations (lines 815, 819) even though line 344 restricts it to display/diagnosis and line 443 bars reducers from consulting clocks, where `created_at` plus `log_index` already suffice; and five-voter support (lines 20, 136-137) multiplies the harness and benchmark matrix (line 824) for a tolerance the doc itself does not recommend (line 136). `inbox/` is already optional (line 393) so cutting it saves little, and replacing per-entry `leader_signature` with a periodic signed chain-head checkpoint is not equivalent - it makes verifying any single exported event require the whole intervening chain, weakening the property claimed at lines 302-305.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The author asked whether V1 can plausibly ship. As written it is a very large V1, and these four items are pure surface area: each one adds canonical-format obligations, golden fixtures, harness scenarios, and security review load without adding a property the design lacks.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a short paragraph to section 13 naming what is explicitly deferred past V1 so scope is visible. Consider dropping `hlc` from the signed event for V1 (keep `created_at` plus `log_index`) and shipping 1 and 3 voters with 5 deferred, noting the harness-matrix saving. Keep the per-entry `leader_signature`: the checkpoint alternative changes the verification property rather than preserving it. `inbox/` may stay as documented-optional.
all_findings.verifier_note: This is opinion within the stated lens rather than a defect, and two of the four cuts are weaker than argued. The `hlc` observation is the strongest: line 328 makes it a signed canonical field while line 344 demotes it to 'display and diagnosis only' and line 443 bars reducers from consulting clocks, so it does carry canonical-encoding, golden-fixture (line 815) and cross-platform-stability (line 819) obligations for no ordering role. The `leader_signature` swap is not equivalent as claimed: with per-entry signatures any single exported event is independently verifiable, whereas a signed periodic chain-head checkpoint requires possession of the whole intervening chain to verify one event - a real reduction in the property at lines 302-305, not the same guarantee cheaper. `inbox/` is already marked 'optional' at line 393 and fully specified in two sentences (lines 426-427), so cutting it removes little. Five voters is a Raft library configuration the doc already de-emphasizes (line 133 'Odd voter counts are preferred', line 136 three 'recommended'); the cost is mostly the harness matrix at line 824. The useful, defensible core is the last sentence of the recommendation: section 13 has no explicit deferral list, so V1 scope is implied rather than visible.

all_findings.title: At-rest posture asserts a requirement it cannot enforce and does not enumerate what sits in the clear
all_findings.problem: Line 713-715 states 'At-rest encryption is not assumed. Require full-disk encryption' without enumerating the cleartext surface that requirement is covering, and without any detection or reporting. CodeComm creates new plaintext copies of repository content outside the workspace that the phrasing does not name: `tmp/` bootstrap staging holding a full verified git bundle (lines 395, 574-575), `conflicts/` resolution snapshots (line 394), and the sidecar's staggered prior-version store (line 601), alongside `state.db`/WAL and `consensus/`. No first-run or `status`/`doctor` check reports FDE state (line 647 covers sync only). Temporary-artifact cleanup is already required at lines 582 and 709; sidecar version retention bounding is not.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The author explicitly asked whether this is an owned tradeoff or a silent gap. It is currently half-owned: the decision is stated, the scope and the enforcement are not, so a reader cannot tell what they are accepting.
all_findings.recommendation: Rewrite lines 713-715 to enumerate the cleartext artifacts CodeComm creates outside the workspace (state.db and WAL, `consensus/`, `logs/`, `conflicts/` snapshots, `tmp/` bootstrap staging including full git bundles, sidecar version history) and note they are new plaintext copies of repository content. Add a first-run and `codecomm status`/`doctor` check that reports per-platform FDE state and warns visibly when it is off, framed as detection rather than enforcement given lines 687-688. Add one clause bounding and making configurable sidecar version retention; temp-artifact expiry is already covered by lines 582 and 709.
all_findings.verifier_note: The central observation is real and correctly rated minor: grep confirms 'full-disk' appears only at line 713, there is no first-run or doctor check for it (line 647 is `sync doctor` only), and the new cleartext locations the reviewer names do exist - tmp bootstrap staging holding a full git bundle (line 395 with 574-575), conflict resolution snapshots (line 394), sidecar staggered versioning of prior file versions outside the repository (line 601). Two sub-claims are already covered, so the finding needs tightening: temporary-artifact hygiene is addressed at line 582 ('delete expired/successful temporary artifacts') and normatively at line 709 ('temporary sensitive artifacts expire securely'), so the reviewer's item (c) is largely redundant for tmp staging - only sidecar version retention bounding is genuinely unstated. Enforcement is also inherently limited: FDE is an OS setting CodeComm can report but not require, and line 687-688 already puts a compromised local OS account outside the V1 boundary, so the realistic ask is detection and disclosure, not enforcement.

all_findings.title: Audit log, activity retention, and data removal have no defined surface, policy, or lifecycle
all_findings.problem: Several user-visible commitments have no defined surface, policy, or lifecycle. Audit: `audit_events` (line 406) and Raft-ordered audit entries (line 128) give tamper-evidence, but no CLI verb exists (lines 637-651), line 631's 'security reviews' view is the control-file surface, and no section enumerates which actions are auditable. Retention: nothing beyond line 58-59 defines how long an ended session's activity, rationale summaries, and path records persist, and there is no delete or further-redact path; compaction appears only as a phase-6 deliverable (line 927). Uninstall is a release-gate word (line 906) with no statement of what it removes. With telemetry off by default (line 706) there is no support-bundle or diagnostics-export path. TUI accessibility is untreated: line 632 requires six states be distinct but nothing requires color-independent encoding or honors NO_COLOR, and line 887 tests only widths, long IDs, and control characters. All license text (lines 710, 760, 878) is dependency review; CodeComm's own license and OSS-distribution posture are absent, which bears on Open Question 5's binary-bundling choice (lines 958-959).
all_findings.why_it_matters: Individually cheap, collectively these are the difference between a design that can be implemented and one where each implementer invents a different answer. The retention and uninstall gaps in particular are user-visible commitments about a tool that durably records everything a human and their agents did to a codebase.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a short section covering: the enumerated set of audited actions plus `codecomm audit list|export`, with one sentence noting the audit log's tamper-evidence derives from the Raft chain and per-entry signature; a retention policy with a default window for ended-session activity and a purge path; a normative statement of what uninstall removes and what it deliberately leaves; a `codecomm support-bundle` producing a redacted user-reviewable archive reusing the line 908 redaction rule; a requirement that all six states at line 632 are distinguishable without color and that NO_COLOR is honored, with a PTY test alongside line 887; and one line naming CodeComm's own license and how it interacts with Open Question 5.
all_findings.verifier_note: Every sub-item checks out against the file, and the severity is honestly rated. (1) `audit_events` exists at line 406 and audit ordering at line 128, but the CLI list at 637-651 has no audit verb and line 631's 'security reviews' view is the control-file review surface (lines 644, 994), not the audit log. (2) No section enumerates which actions are auditable; the only concrete hits are line 660 and line 183. (3) Retention beyond line 58-59's 'session-lifetime coordination history with export before compaction' is undefined - compaction appears only as a phase-6 deliverable (line 927) with no post-session retention or delete path. (4) Uninstall appears only as a release-gate word (line 906) with no statement of what it removes. (5) Telemetry is off by default (line 706) and there is no diagnostics/support-bundle path; line 647 is `sync doctor` and line 908 is a test-artifact redaction rule. (6) grep finds no NO_COLOR or color-independence requirement anywhere, while line 632 requires six states be distinct and line 887 tests only widths, long IDs, and control characters. (7) All three license hits (710, 760, 878) are dependency license review; CodeComm's own license and distribution posture are absent, which does bear on Open Question 5 (lines 958-959). Bundling seven separate gaps into one finding is poor form, but each is individually true and the collective 'each implementer invents a different answer' consequence is fair.

all_findings.title: The unasked question: is CodeComm one person with several devices, or several people? The doc never says, and the answer changes half the design
all_findings.problem: There is no user/person/principal identity anywhere in the document. The identifier table (150-159) has device, session, workspace, agent-profile, agent-session, and event IDs — no human. Roles (4.2) are granted to devices, not people. Yet the document silently assumes both models in different places. Multi-human is assumed at line 223-224 ("Both users compare and confirm a short authentication string" — a solo user pairing their own two laptops performs both halves of a two-sided ceremony alone, which is not a ceremony), at line 183 ("cannot be self-granted" — vacuous if one human owns every device), at 684 ("workspace readability by authorized owner/editors" listed as a threat-model condition, which only means anything between distinct people), and at 179-181 (owner approves editor proposals). Single-human is assumed at 12/43 ("per-user daemon"), at 442 ("cannot stop a same-user process from editing a path"), at 688 (compromised local OS account out of scope), and by the entire at-rest posture at 713-715. Open Question 4 asks whether 2-8 devices is representative but never asks how many humans those devices belong to. Section 15 contains no question on this at all.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This single unresolved question determines: whether the role model needs a user layer at all or is over-built; whether pairing needs two-sided out-of-band confirmation or is theater; whether the audit log has any purpose; whether "cannot be self-granted", revocation, and Byzantine-voter exclusions are meaningful controls or decoration; whether at-rest encryption is optional (my own laptops) or mandatory (my teammate's disk holds my code); whether conflict resolution UX is single-operator or negotiated; and whether the product is "my agents follow me across my machines" or "my team's agents share a workspace". Roughly a third of the mechanisms in sections 4, 8.4, and 10 are priced for the multi-human case while the narrative voice ("per-user daemon", "same-user process") is the single-human case. Every other reviewer critiqued mechanisms; none asked who the mechanisms are for.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a section 2.0 stating the user model explicitly, with a named primary persona and a named excluded one, e.g. "V1 target: one developer, 2-8 devices they personally control; multi-human sessions are supported opportunistically but the trust model assumes all owner/editor devices are equally trusted by one person." Then re-derive: if single-human, cut or downgrade two-sided SAS confirmation, self-grant prevention, and per-device role separation, and state that authorized-member confidentiality is explicitly not a goal. If multi-human, add a `user_id` (or account) identifier, bind roles to users rather than devices, and add the missing threat: authorized-but-distrusted teammate. Add this as Open Question 0 with a decision deadline before phase 1 exits.

all_findings.title: Daemon-to-session cardinality is contradictory: "per-user daemon" vs per-workspace lock, per-session sidecar, and a single IPC socket
all_findings.problem: Line 12/43 specify one long-lived daemon per user. Line 654-655 specifies "a per-workspace OS lock [that] prevents two local daemons owning the same DB/sidecar home" — which presupposes multiple daemons per user, one per workspace. Line 533 pins one Syncthing sidecar per session. All state lives under a workspace-relative `.codecomm/` (388-396) containing exactly one `session.json`, one `state.db`, and one `consensus/` directory, so the schema is single-session. The MCP process "reaches the owner-restricted daemon through a Unix socket or Windows named pipe" (456-459) — singular, with no addressing scheme for choosing among several. The discovery datagram carries one `session_id` (195) and credential epochs are per-session (235-255). Nothing states whether a user may participate in two sessions or two workspaces at once, whether that means two daemons, two sockets, two Raft clusters, two sidecars, and two multicast advertisers per interface, or whether the 32-agent and 2-8-device caps (45) are per session, per workspace, or per host.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A developer working on two repositories concurrently is the ordinary case, not an edge case. Which cardinality is chosen determines the process model, the IPC namespace and discovery mechanism the CLI/TUI/MCP adapters use, the on-disk layout of global identity vs per-session state (401), whether one device identity key is shared across sessions (it is, per 152/164 — so two sessions share an identity but not a credential epoch), the number of multicast advertisers and listening ports per host, resource budgets, and the meaning of the service targets. This is upstream of nearly every implementation task in section 13 phase 2 and is not resolvable from the text.
all_findings.recommendation: State the cardinality explicitly in section 3's component table: e.g. "one `codecommd` per (user, session); the client discovers running daemons via a per-user registry directory under the platform-standard config location; `codecomm`/MCP select one with `--session` or by workspace-root ancestry." Then reconcile line 12/43 wording, define the socket-naming/discovery scheme for local clients, scope the 2-8 device and 32-agent caps to a named unit, and state the supported number of concurrent sessions per host with its resource implications.

all_findings.title: No human-override or stuck-work recovery surface: a task claimed by a dead agent session stays claimed forever, and no CLI/MCP verb can release it
all_findings.problem: Line 496 states that agent-session expiry "ends the session, releases leases, and forbids ID reuse" — leases are released, task claims are not. Task ownership is `(device_id, agent_session_id)` (432), and `agent_session_id` is never reused (156, 496), so a task in `claimed`/`in_progress`/`blocked` whose owning agent session has ended is permanently owned by an identity that can never return, and the compare-and-set reducer will presumably reject transitions proposed by anyone else. Correspondingly, the entire mutation surface is one-directional: the MCP verbs are `task.list/claim/update`, `lease.acquire/renew`, `plan.get/propose`, `memory.append`, `activity.append` (466-470) — no unclaim, reassign, lease.release, memory tombstone, or plan rollback; the CLI is `task add|claim|start|block|done` and `agent list|launch|publish` (639-641) — no `agent stop`, no `task unclaim|reassign|cancel|delete`, no `lease release|break`, no way for a member to depart voluntarily (only `peer revoke`, 645). The failure table (657-676) covers 21 infrastructure failures and zero human-intervention scenarios: no row for "agent is doing the wrong thing", "work is stuck", "task owner is gone", or "user wants to abandon a claim", despite risk 7 (973-974) stating agents may simply ignore the workflow.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is a liveness defect reachable by the single most common event in the system — an agent process exiting. Every affected task becomes permanently unworkable with no documented remedy, and because completion is additionally blocked by unresolved conflicts (600) the same dead-end applies to `sync_blocked` work. More broadly, a coordination tool for autonomous agents whose only human verbs are "start more work" is missing the half of the interface operators will use most: stop, take back, redo, hand off. The consistency lens noted that no verb leaves `blocked`; the wider absence of any override/abort/reassign model, and the specific dead-owner claim leak, are unaddressed.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a subsection 6.3 "Ownership release and operator override" specifying: (a) claim release on agent-session end — either automatic (reducer releases claims when the committed agent-session-ended event applies, returning the task to `ready` with a recorded reason) or explicit; (b) an owner/editor force-release and reassign command that is a committed, audited event with expected-version semantics; (c) `agent stop`, `task unclaim|reassign|cancel`, `lease release`, and `peer leave` in the CLI table, with which of them are deliberately absent from MCP so agents cannot self-authorize them; and (d) failure-table rows for dead task owner, runaway agent, and abandoned worktree.

all_findings.title: The domain model — tasks, plans, memory, leases — is eight bullets with no fields, bounds, or relations, while engineering hygiene gets 190 lines
all_findings.problem: Section 6.2 defines the entire application domain in eight bullets. There is not one field of a task, plan revision, memory record, or lease anywhere in the document: no title/description/size limits, no priority or ordering, no parent/child or dependency relations, no assignee vs owner distinction, no acceptance criteria, no plan-to-task linkage, no memory record shape or scope/key model, no lease glob syntax or maximum duration, no task-to-conflict or task-to-worktree relation. The event envelope (307-340) types every metadata field but leaves `payload: {}` and `actions: []` opaque, and `entity_id`/`expected_entity_version` have no per-entity semantics. Section 12.2 then requires unit coverage of "task/plan states" (803) and golden fixtures for canonical events (816) for entities that are never specified. By contrast, sections 11 and 12 spend 190 lines on generic production-engineering and testing practice that is not specific to this product.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The payload of every replicated event, every reducer, every projection table, every MCP tool schema, every TUI view, and every golden fixture is derived from these entity definitions. Nothing in sections 5-9, 12, or 13 can be built or tested without them, so the document's implementation-ready surface is inverted: the commodity parts (Raft usage, TLS, testing policy) are specified in depth and the differentiated product is a sketch. It also means reviewers cannot evaluate whether the product actually coordinates agents usefully — the reader learns how a task transition is committed but never what a task is.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a section 6.0 "Domain model" with a typed schema per entity (fields, required/optional, size and cardinality bounds, relations, and which fields are reducer-validated vs display-only), plus the per-kind `payload` schema for each event kind in the registry. Reference it from the MCP tool schemas (466-470) and the golden fixtures (816-820). Consider moving the generic parts of section 11 to an engineering-standards appendix so the body's proportions match where the risk actually is.

all_findings.title: Roaming, sleep/wake, and address change — the normal life of a laptop on a LAN — have no design treatment anywhere
all_findings.problem: Section 2.2 covers which networks work but never covers a network changing. Peer endpoints come from committed roster "endpoint hints" (276) and multicast, and line 207 states the source address is only a hint — but nothing specifies how a peer's address is updated when it changes, whether address changes are committed events, how a device re-establishes direct connections and Syncthing tunnels after DHCP renewal, Wi-Fi-to-Ethernet switch, VPN reconnect, or laptop suspend/resume, or how long stale hints are retried before falling back to multicast. The failure table (657-676) has no row for "peer address changed", "host suspended", or "interface disappeared". Sleep/wake appears exactly once in the document — as a native test-matrix item (885) — with no requirement for it to test against. Multicast advertisement is `MAY` (188) with a jittered but unnumbered interval, so it is not a reliable re-discovery mechanism, and the manual-endpoint fallback (211) is a human action.
all_findings.why_it_matters: For a local-first tool on developer laptops, address change and suspend/resume are the dominant availability events — far more frequent than voter loss or DB corruption, both of which get dedicated treatment. Unhandled, they produce exactly the failure the design most wants to avoid: peers that are physically reachable but stay disconnected until a user manually re-enters an endpoint, plus stalled Syncthing tunnels, expiring credential epochs during suspend (a laptop closed for 40 minutes wakes with expired credentials and, if quorum is elsewhere and unreachable, into the renewal-only path), and elections triggered by a sleeping voter. The 30-minute credential epoch and suspend/resume interact directly and neither section 4.5 nor section 9 mentions it.
all_findings.recommendation: Add a subsection to 2.2 or 4.3 covering endpoint churn: make address change an observable local event that triggers re-advertisement and peer reconnect; specify whether endpoint hints are committed state or gossip, with a TTL and refresh rule; give the multicast interval a value and make advertisement `MUST` on selected interfaces; specify reconnect backoff and tunnel re-establishment. Add failure-table rows for host suspend/resume, interface change, and address change, and state the required behavior for waking with an expired credential epoch while quorum is unreachable.

all_findings.title: Named replicated state has no persistence home: activity and acknowledgements are 2.1 goals, credential authorizations and control-file proposals are committed Raft state, and none appears in the table list
all_findings.problem: Goal line 48 requires replicating "ordered plans, tasks, memory, leases, activity, and acknowledgements". The core table list (405-407) is `schema_migrations, consensus_state, events, idempotency_keys, devices, agent_sessions, tasks, plan_revisions, memory_records, leases, replication_cursors, outbox, sync_conflicts, audit_events` — there is no activity table (activity is a view at 437 and an MCP verb at 469, and `audit_events` is described separately at 128 as durable audit, not agent activity) and no acknowledgement/peer-watermark table, though `POST /v1/acks` is specified as a "durable applied watermark" (285) and peer watermarks are a required view (437, 679). Section 128 lists "credential-key authorizations" as Raft-ordered durable state and 4.5 specifies their contents, but there is no credential/authorization table, and 248 requires peers to look up "that index" and confirm an active key digest — a query against state that has no declared home. Section 8.4 creates committed `control_file.change_proposed` events with per-device local approval (617-619) and there is no proposals or approvals table, so local approval decisions have no stated durability. Membership/roles/voters are presumably in `devices`, but that is never said.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Two named 2.1 goals (activity, acknowledgements) have no delivering mechanism in section 6, which breaks goal-to-section traceability; and two pieces of security-critical committed state — the credential authorization set that every mTLS handshake validates against, and per-device control-file approvals — have no projection, so the reducer and the TLS verification path in 4.5 step 6 cannot be implemented as written. This also silently changes the reviewer's mental model of what is authoritative: is agent activity durable replicated state or an ephemeral view?
all_findings.recommendation: Add the missing tables (`activity_events` or an explicit statement that activity is a projection over `events`; `peer_acks`; `credential_authorizations`; `control_file_proposals` and `control_file_approvals`; and explicit membership/role/voter columns or tables), and add a short goals-to-sections traceability table mapping each 2.1 bullet to the section and table that delivers it, so gaps like activity and acknowledgements surface mechanically.

all_findings.title: Section 14 is unfalsifiable as written: undefined measurement points, a self-cancelling final line, no gate references it, and zero resource budgets for a laptop-resident daemon
all_findings.problem: Four problems compound. (a) The latency targets name no measurement endpoints: "connected coordination visibility p95 <500 ms" does not say from what event (MCP call accepted? Raft commit? local apply on the peer? TUI render?) to what, at what offered load, on what workload, with how many devices and agents. "Stable file visibility p95 <2 s" does not define "stable" or the file size. (b) Line 946 — "Targets require benchmark validation before commitment" — withdraws the section's normative force entirely, so nothing here can fail. (c) Section 12.5's release gate (904-909) lists no numeric threshold from section 14; the benchmark list (889-891) tracks throughput and catch-up dimensions that section 14 does not mention and omits every latency target section 14 does state, so the two sections do not join up. (d) Lines 939-944 are not targets at all — they are restatements of the 2.4 invariants (durability, exactly-one-winner, no reachable local API) placed in a latency section. (e) There is no resource target of any kind: the words CPU, memory footprint, RSS, disk space, and battery appear nowhere in the document, for a design that runs a permanent background daemon plus a Syncthing sidecar plus up to 28 tunnels and 32 agent sessions on a developer's laptop, and stores session-lifetime history (58) with compaction that has no retention floor.
all_findings.why_it_matters: As written, section 14 cannot be passed or failed, so it provides no acceptance criteria and no design pressure. Meanwhile, the target most likely to determine whether developers keep the tool installed — idle and active CPU, memory, disk growth, and battery cost of a permanently running daemon plus sidecar — is entirely unbudgeted, and unbudgeted background resource use is the classic failure mode for local-first developer daemons. Splitting invariants into a targets list also weakens both: the invariants lose their status and the targets lose their coherence.
all_findings.recommendation: Rewrite section 14 as a table with columns for metric, precise start and end measurement points, workload and topology, threshold, and the gate in 12.5 that enforces it; delete line 946 or replace it with a dated commitment ("provisional until phase 3 benchmarks; each value MUST be confirmed or revised with recorded evidence before phase 6"). Move lines 939-944 into 2.4 as invariants. Add explicit resource budgets: idle and active daemon CPU and RSS ceilings, sidecar overhead, `.codecomm/` disk growth per 10k events with a retention floor, and battery-impact expectations on macOS and Windows; wire them into the nightly performance tier.

all_findings.title: The 2.4 invariant table is insufficient for the 2.1 goals: no durability invariant, no confidentiality invariant, and three rows whose "enforcement" only restates the invariant
all_findings.problem: Eleven invariants, all negative safety properties about state and control flow.
