Missing relative to the goals: (a) durability — "no acknowledged event loss" is the property the whole persistence design exists for, and it appears only as a section 14 bullet (939) and test scenario 18 (859), never as an invariant, even though 6.1 line 363-364 specifies the single-transaction mechanism that enforces it; (b) idempotent resumption (goal line 53) has no invariant despite being the stated basis of every recovery path; (c) distinct durable identity (goal 46-47) is covered only obliquely by the anti-spoofing row, not by a uniqueness/non-reuse invariant, though 412-415 enforces exactly that; (d) no confidentiality invariant — nothing states that workspace content, secrets, or activity never leave the authorized member set, despite that being the point of sections 8.4, 10, and the discovery-privacy claims. Separately, three rows have an enforcement column that restates the invariant instead of naming a mechanism: "No permanent routing node | Every authorized pair connects directly", "No remote agent control | MCP is local stdio; peer API has no execution primitive" (an assertion about the API, not an enforcement point), and "No private reasoning capture | Store rationale summaries and redacted activity only" (a policy, not an enforcement).
all_findings.why_it_matters: The invariant table is the document's contract — it is what section 11 line 765 tells implementers to document and what section 12 is supposed to test against. Properties absent from it get treated as best-effort: durability and idempotent resume are the two properties whose violation causes silent data loss, and neither is listed. Rows whose enforcement is a restatement give false assurance that a checkable mechanism exists; a reviewer or implementer cannot derive a test from them. This directly answers the question of whether 2.4 suffices for 2.1: it does not.
all_findings.recommendation: Add invariants for durability ("No acknowledged event is lost | Event, projection, idempotency result, and applied index commit in one SQLite transaction with full durability"), idempotent resumption, identity uniqueness and non-reuse, and content confidentiality; and replace the three restated enforcement cells with the specific code-level enforcement point and the test in section 12 that proves it. Add a column linking each invariant to its enforcing section and its regression scenario.

all_findings.title: Open Questions are load-bearing on choices sections 1 and 2.1 already present as decided, and neither questions nor risks have an owner, deadline, or mitigation status
all_findings.problem: Section 1 is titled "Decision Summary" and section 2.1 states goals as `MUST`, but section 15 leaves several of those same items open. OQ2 ("May editors select current plan?") contradicts line 180's committed capability matrix entry ("No by default") and 432-433's plan semantics. OQ1 (ongoing Git) is presented as open while 8.3 line 594 already specifies conditional behavior and line 26 commits to bundle bootstrap. OQ4 asks whether 2-8 devices, 100k files, 2 GiB, and 100 MiB/file are representative, while line 45 makes those exact numbers a `MUST` and line 58 a target — so a `MUST` in section 2 is contingent on an open question in section 15, and sections 12.3/12.4 already build benchmarks and harness caps around them. OQ5 (sidecar distribution) blocks phase 5 and section 10's supply-chain controls. None of the five questions has an owner, a decision deadline, a decision procedure, or a named consequence of each answer; none is tied to a phase in section 13, and section 13 has no gate requiring open questions to be closed before the dependent phase starts. Section 16's ten risks likewise have no owner, likelihood, mitigation status, or trigger/early-warning signal, and several restate content from section 10 rather than tracking exposure.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A reader cannot tell which parts of the document are settled. Presenting contingent items in a table headed "V1 decision" and as `MUST` goals overstates convergence to the Product half of the stated audience, and understates it for implementers, who will build against numbers and behaviors that are still in play. Without owners or deadlines, open questions do not get closed; without triggers, risks are not monitored. This is a document-governance gap distinct from the previously noted absence of authors and changelog.
all_findings.recommendation: Mark every section 1 row and 2.1 bullet that depends on an unresolved question with a provisional flag and a cross-reference to its OQ number; give each open question an owner, a decision deadline expressed as a section 13 phase gate, a decision procedure, and a one-line statement of what changes under each answer. Give each risk an owner, current mitigation status, and an observable trigger. Add "all open questions blocking this phase are closed" to each phase's exit criteria.

all_findings.title: Section 11 declares ~40 production requirements to be "a release criterion" but no gate in 12.5 or section 13 verifies any of them
all_findings.problem: Line 732 states "Production quality is a release criterion" and then lists roughly forty requirements, many of which are mechanically checkable — acyclic module dependencies and explicit boundaries (734-735), decode-once into bounded typed structures (736-738), no panic on peer/repository/input errors (739-740), deadline and cancellation propagation through every boundary (741), bounded queues, bodies, retries, connections, caches, and child resources (741-742), no silent dropping of durable work (743), atomic replacement with explicit modes and canonical paths (747-748), redacting secret types with no secrets in URLs/argv/logs (752-753), and no ignored errors in security/durability/process/network paths with every suppression carrying reason, owner, and review (762-764). Section 12.5's per-PR gate lists format/lint/static/dependency policy, tests, race detection, contract/golden/migration, bounded multi-daemon, same-device multi-agent, security regression, and coverage floors — none of which maps to any of the above except by hope. The release gate (904-909) adds no boundary, resource-bound, panic-freedom, or cancellation checks. Section 13 assigns none of them to a phase.
all_findings.why_it_matters: An unverified "release criterion" is not a criterion; as written, section 11 is unfalsifiable and will be satisfied by assertion at release time. The specific items at risk are the ones that cause the failures this design fears most: an unbounded queue or missing cancellation path turns a slow peer into a daemon OOM, a panic on malformed peer input turns a hostile-LAN packet into a denial of service on every member, and an ignored error on the durability path silently violates the durability property (which, per NEW-8, is also not an invariant).
all_findings.recommendation: Convert the checkable subset of section 11 into named gates in 12.5 with the enforcing tool (import-cycle/architecture lint, `errcheck`/`lostcancel`/`nilerr`-class linters, panic-recovery boundary tests driven by the existing fuzz corpus, a resource-bound conformance test asserting every listed bound has a configured value, a secrets-in-argv/env/log artifact scan). For the judgement-based remainder, state explicitly that they are enforced by the focused review requirement at 768-771 and name the reviewer role. Add a phase-0 or phase-1 task that stands up the architecture and error-handling lints so the boundaries are enforced from the first commit rather than retrofitted in phase 6.
